utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone after a relatively long time. We are here to hear the final argument. The parties have filed their final briefs, and an opportunity is given to them to further plead their cases, but before we do so, I have a few, really a very few, practical matters to deal with. First one is the registrar - and this should be on the record now - the registrar has vacated P1124, P1125, P1128, and P1132 because they were identical to other exhibits that were already admitted into evidence. It's now on the record. Second item concerns a video which was played in court on the 20th of August, 2007, and the 22nd of August of that same year. On those days the Prosecutor put in court a video to Witness Dunjic who has commented on it. The video was referred to and introduced as being V000/6012 -- I made a mistake, it's now well on the record - being P452; however, there is an inconsistency because P452 is V000/6011. The correct exhibit number of the video introduced as V000/6012 is D66. This correction is made so that it is on the record that not P452, but instead D66 was played and put to the Witness Dunjic on the 20th and the 22nd of August, 2007. I move on to the next item which concerns Exhibit Number P921. Due to a technical error, P921, which was used by the Prosecution with Witness Rade Repic was incorrectly marked in e-court as being admitted. For this reason it did not appear on the Chamber's record as requiring clarification from the parties during the last housekeeping session. The Prosecution has at no time pressed for its admission. The documents contained in the exhibit are statements not taken for the purpose of legal proceedings before the Tribunal, but they do concern acts and conducts of the accused. As is explained in the decision of this Chamber of the 29th of November, 2007, in relation to the documents tendered during the testimony of Witness Stijovic, and I specifically draw your attention to paragraph 11 of that decision, documents of the kind of P922 [sic] are not to be admitted into evidence. Therefore, the Chamber, in view of what it considered in paragraph 11 of this decision of the 29th of December [sic], 2007, is not inclined to admit P921 into evidence and corrects the status of this exhibit as being marked for identification and not admitted into evidence. I move on to the public versions of 92 ter statements. An e-mail has been sent to the parties dealing with the question how public versions of 92 bis and 92 ter statements should be made accessible to the public. The next item deals with the testimony of Witness Fazliu. The Chamber has invited the parties to agree on what portions of the testimony of the transcript of Mr. Fazliu could be made public. The Chamber has received no input from the parties; therefore, we could not establish whether there was any agreement. The parties received an e-mail today in which they're again invited to reach an agreement, but not only that the Chamber even has made a proposal in that e-mail for the parties to consider whether they can agree on it or not. The parties are invited to see whether they can reach an agreement and inform the Chamber not later than Wednesday, this Wednesday, and before we adjourn so that the Chamber could, if there's agreement but even if there's no agreement, that the Chamber could give an order to the registry to make public certain portions of the evidence of the Witness Fazliu. Last point I have on my list is the filing of revised briefs that include corrigenda. It has been suggested that together with corrigenda a new revised brief would be filed. The Chamber for several reasons has turned down such a suggestion and will continue to do so. Of course corrigenda should be filed, but both for very practical reasons such as from what copy of the final brief we're working, on what copy you've made your annotations; but apart from that, also for reasons of several thousands of pages to be reproduced, people working on it, distributing it, and we're really talking about many, many thousand of pages if a document of some 400 pages would have to be refiled and redistributed. For that reason, the Chamber, although it fully understands that -- I think especially Defence of Mr. Haradinaj would prefer to have the perfect versions on the record, that for these practical purposes the Chamber denies any further suggestions in that respect. I can add to that that if I would have made a mistake I also would very much like to have a fully correct version filed, but sometimes we have to live with the imperfect. These were the practical matters I wanted to raise before I give an opportunity to the parties to -- for closing arguments. The time schedule has been: Prosecution, three hours; Defence, four and a half hours in total; Prosecution's rebuttal argument, one hour; Defence rejoinder arguments, one and a half hours. I'll strictly keep you to the time-limits. Yes, whether I misspoke or whether it's not correctly put on the record, page 2, line 16, a reference was made to "P921" where it reads "P922." And page 2, line 19, if I referred to the 29th of December, 2007, then it was a mistake because it should be the 29th of November, 2007. This being corrected, I give an opportunity to you, Mr. Re, to present final arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before commencing, could I briefly announce the appearance of the Prosecution lawyers here. There's a reason. I have a new lawyer who hasn't been introduced before. David Re, with trial attorneys, Gramsci Di Fazio; Philip Kearney; Gilles Dutertre; Legal Officers, Katrina Gustafson, Rut Ley; Associate Legal Officer, Romana Schweiger, and introducing to the Court Mr. Will Bryne, Assistant Legal Officer, who's not wearing a robe. That's who's here present in court. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, and although at a late stage, welcome in court for -- for you Mr. Bryne Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Also to assist the Court we'll be using PowerPoint and showing some exhibits and transcript excerpts which we will do in Sanction, so I will cue that at the appropriate moment so that can be displayed. Now, we come to the end of the trial and after hearing days of evidence, almost a hundred witnesses, almost 11.000 pages of transcript, the Prosecution has concluded its case and, we submit, it has overwhelming proved the guilt of the three accused, Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj and Lahi Brahimaj of the crimes charged. They are guilty of the crimes of persecution as a crime against humanity and the various other charges of crimes against humanity and the alternative charges or the other charges of war crimes. The Prosecution submits that for every count it has charged it has proved the guilt of the accused. What I want to start with is to take the Court, take the Trial Chamber, which has heard all the evidence to the similarities in this case. This case is a case of similarities, and these similarities are those which will convict Haradinaj, Balaj, and Brahimaj of persecution as a crime against humanity. The similarities are these: The victims all fell within a pattern. Serb civilians left behind after the remainder of the Serb population were expelled from Haradinaj's Dukagjini zone by Easter 1998. Alleged or perceived Serbian spies or collaborators. The bodies fit a pattern. The bodies were found together. Their injuries had a similar pattern, they bore similar marks of mistreatment consistent with torture, cruel treatment, and injuries you would expect to find if people had been detained and tortured. Of the 31 bodies found in the canal, 20 of those victims had died of gun-shot wounds and the Defence does not dispute that. The bodies were found in an isolated area next to Balaj's Black Eagles training ground. That particular piece of land, isolated patch, is 1.94 kilometres in a straight line from Haradinaj's house in an area that was then at the time the bodies were dumped was firmly under Haradinaj's control. Another similarity is that the bodies were found in virtually the order in which they had been abducted or disappeared. We submit that there are too many bodies of too many similar people, Serb civilians, civilians on KLA wanted lists, Roma, alleged or perceived collaborators, for it to have happened by chance. The bodies of two victims abducted by Balaj personally were found together at the canal, that was the mother and sister of Witness 4. The body of another last seen heading in the direction of the canal, that's Sanije Balaj, was in the back of his jeep. Balaj was taking the body in that direction and her body was found directly on top of those two other people who had been kidnapped by Balaj some months before. The body of the victim Pal Krasniqi, who was tortured most grievously in Brahimaj's detention centre at Jablanica, was found next to a victim, Sali Berisha, whose father Misin was on a KLA wanted list. There are simply too many similarities here for these acts to be random. There are far too many coincidences for these crimes to have occurred by chance by actors unknown to each other acting alone. The only conclusion is that they must have occurred pursuant to a common criminal purpose. There is no other explanation. The area was then firmly under Haradinaj's control. The murders, abductions, tortures, and other crimes are pleaded, and we submit proved, could not have occurred without Haradinaj's knowledge or his complicity. It is so important that the Trial Chamber views the evidence in its totality and not as Haradinaj's counsel submits or ask you to, to try and examine each count separately and to base your decision upon looking at each case separately and in isolation because it's only when you view the entirety of the evidence against the three accused, each count, and you put them together, that the evidence of the pattern emerges. It's then that you begin to see the whole picture. Once you see the whole picture you understand the impossibility of these 40 murders occurring by chance or by coincidence. They simply could not have. It's also very important to view the persecution pleaded in the indictment and proved at trial in the historical context of the events in Kosovo at the time with the military development of the KLA. As we've set out in our brief in the introduction, in the background section, 1998 was a year of enormous turmoil in Kosovo. Albania was in chaos, its economy in ruins, its armouries looted, and weapons were flooding across the border into Kosovo. Against that background, the Serbian authorities were taking increasingly legally repressive measures against the province's overwhelmingly Albanian population. It is fair to say that Kosovo at the time was awash with weapons. It was against this that the Kosovo Liberation Army, known as the KLA or UCK, seized its opportunity. But what had it been doing for the previous four or five years? In that time, the KLA had been mounting low-level terrorist attacks against the Serbian state, its supporters, and civilians. In that period, the KLA had killed police, attacked police stations, assassinated municipal officials, and attacked Serbian refugee settlements, such as that at Babaloc, and the Trial Chamber has heard evidence of the KLA attacks on Babaloc during the indictment period. But after attacking, murdering, blowing up various Serb civilians and state officials, the KLA proudly claimed responsibility in a series of communiques it was issuing from 1994 through to 1998. It actually took responsibility for the murder of Serb civilians as a kind of warning to those who were living there. And it was in 1998 with access to the Albanian weapons cache flowing across the border that the KLA seized its opportunity to mount an armed struggle against the Serbian authorities. Attacks escalated and the KLA organized itself militarily. And then for the first time it represented a real military threat to Serbia. Now, Serbia's response was increasing force and escalating human rights abuses, leading to the KLA in turn to retaliate and then a vicious cycle or circle of violence developed with both sides retaliating against each other with increasing force. The evidence has proved beyond reasonable doubt that - and without any serious challenge from the accused - that by at least mid-April 1998, an armed conflict had developed in the area of the subject of the indictment. Unfortunately, as in many wars, civilians were the victim of the -- were the victims of the armed conflict that developed in this area by at least mid-1998, and in this particular conflict both sides committed atrocities against the civilian population, both sides committed crimes of persecution and other crimes against humanity and breaches of the laws of war, similar to those pleaded in this indictment. But the evidence establishes that the attacks against the civilians in the Dukagjini area were particularly vicious and the conflict came to involve, like many of the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia, what is colloquially known as the ethnic cleansing of civilians from opposing sides. But justice must be blind and perpetrators on both sides to the conflict have stood trial before this Tribunal. Unfortunately for the civilians, Serb civilians and perceived opponents of the KLA, KLA members in the Dukagjin area led by Ramush Haradinaj combined their armed struggle against the Serbian state with an attack upon part of the civilian population. It was an attack against Serb civilians generally and against Kosovo Albanians and Roma and other civilians who were or were perceived to be -- even perceived to be collaborating with the Serbian forces or opposing the KLA. In 1998, the evidence has firmly established that the three accused were members of the joint criminal enterprise pleaded in the indictment. The common criminal purpose was the KLA consolidating control over the Dukagjini area, but doing so by unlawfully expelling or mistreating Serbs and other civilians perceived to be collaborating with the Serbian regime or otherwise opposed to the KLA. Haradinaj, Balaj, Brahimaj, and other participants in this enterprise, including Haradinaj's and Brahimaj's brothers, enthusiastically and without mercy implemented its common criminal purpose. Long-time Serb families were expelled from their homes. Serb civilians were targeted for mistreatment, they were abducted, they were murdered. Suspected collaborators were hunted down and were murdered. By mid-April 1998, most of the Serb population had been driven out of the area following the sustained attacks, violence and persecution directed against them by those acting according to the common criminal purpose. As you heard during the evidence, the KLA used a compound deep within its stronghold of Jablanica to detain and torture prisoners. The accused, Lahi Brahimaj, had his own room there and personally participated in the torture and mistreatment of KLA prisoners. Wanted lists and black lists of suspected collaborators were created. The names of these people were circulated at KLA staff meetings and among KLA village guards monitoring the numerous check-points set up in the region. If captured, the fate of those on the list was near certain death. The following seven victims listed in the indictment, of which you've heard evidence, were all on KLA black lists or were otherwise wanted. I say "wanted" by the KLA. That's Istref and Nurija Krasniqi, counts 21 and 22; Zenun Gashi, counts 19, 20; Misin Berisha, counts 19 and 20; Skender Kuci, counts 31 and 32; Sejd Noci, counts 21, 22; Witness 3, counts 31, 32; and Sanije Balaj, Counts 21, 22. The Baran valley KLA command which reported to Haradinaj circulated a wanted list naming alleged collaborators Istref and Nurije Krasniqi, Zenun Gashi, Misin Berisha, and Skender Kuci, and all five were abducted and murdered by the KLA. The bodies of Istref and Nurije Krasniqi, Zenun Gashi, Misin Berisha and his two sons were found within metres of each other at the canal. Haradinaj appointed Balaj, also known as -- or known to everyone at the time as Toger, the lieutenant, to command a particularly notorious KLA unit called the Black Eagles. This 30-or-so strong unit terrorised its victims throughout the indictment period. Balaj reported directly to Haradinaj. Balaj had his own personal black list kept in a notebook he carried with him while looking for people on it. Balaj and Haradinaj frequently met; they worked together. Balaj personally raped one victim and abducted others. Balaj's unit trained and was based right next to the canal where the bodies were found. As I mentioned before, the family compound of the Haradinaj clan is a mere less than 2 kilometres across open country from the canal. The main feature in 1998 when the bodies were dumped there between the Haradinaj family compound and the canal was Balaj's Black Eagles training site. The bodies -- the evidence has proved that at least 40 victims of the joint criminal enterprise were murdered in the indictment period. The bodies of at least 31 of these were found at and down stream for an obvious execution site at the canal that were found there in September 1998. The three accused do not contest that 20 of them died from gun-shot wounds. The bodies of two missing Serb victims were found in the shallow roadside grave also in KLA-controlled Dashinoc. The KLA controlled the canal area from April 1998, coinciding with the disappearance of the victims whose bodies were found there until Serbian forces temporarily regained control of the territory in September 1998 and made the particularly gruesome discovery of the bodies. The KLA had a long-standing policy of attacking Serb civilians and those it considered cooperating with the Serbian authorities. The Trial Chamber can consider the evidence of the KLA's attacks on Serb civilians and collaborators as evidence of the mens rea, that's the intention, the persecutor intention of them the KLA participants in the localised joint criminal enterprise in the Dukagjini zone in 1998. Now, the KLA communiques issued in -- between 1994 and 1998 make very, very chilling reading. In evidence, if this could be displayed in Sanction, is a KLA communique, number 13, of June 1995. Now, in that, as you can see on the screen, it refers, first of all, to an attack upon a Serbian police station in April, but then, in a far more sinister fashion it goes on: "Two houses recently built for Serb and Montenegrin colonizers were mined in the beginning of May. The explosions in Junik are a warning to the colonizers which accept to comply with the ethnic cleansing exercised by Belgrade." It then goes on: "The Serbian spy Bexhet Mucaku was assassinated the last week of May." And finally in a very chilling and sinister warning to the minority Serbian population in Kosovo: "We appeal to the Serbian civil population to think carefully about their future in Kosovo and not participate in the occupying military and police troops organized against Albanians!" Now, Zoran Stijovic, who was the chief Serbian state security analyst in Pristina testified, both to the accuracy of these communiques and the fact that the things which they had spoken about happened. Another one which bears dwelling on for a moment was issued on the 20th of November, 1997, a few months before the armed conflict in the Dukagjini area in Kosovo, communique number 39. And it refers specifically to the KLA central staff carrying out "an armed operation on Qamil Gashi ... After several unsuccessful warnings were given to him regarding the damages he had caused to the national issue. He was a parliament member of Serbia, official of Serb Socialist Confederation of the Municipality of Gllogovc and a missionary of the Serb invader against the civilian war." Now these communiques, and there are many of them, quite eloquently demonstrate the persecutor intention of the KLA and its members towards Serb civilians by making deliberate attacks on people they considered to be collaborators with the Serbian state. The attacks continued. Mr. Stijovic testified in this trial of an enormous increase in the number of attacks between 1992 and 1998. In his statement in evidence, Exhibit P931, at paragraph 20, he describes the attacks increasing from eight in 1992 to 11 in 1993, four in 1994, nine in 1995, 31 in 1996, 75 in 1997, and through to 30th of November, 1998, some 1.486 attacks. As he describes at the beginning of that paragraph: "The terrorist attacks in 1995, 1996, and 1997, against the police and against Albanians who did not support the agenda of the separatists increased dramatically." His further tabulation is shown at paragraph 62 of his statement, also in evidence at Exhibit P931, in which he broke down the 1486 attacks until 30th of November, 1996. He tabulated the deaths of 90 Albanian and Serbian citizens, 105 MUP members, and 37 VJ, that's Serbian or FRY military members, 481 people were wounded, of whom 96 were civilians, 283 were MUP, and 102 were VJ. But during the same period and consistent with the evidence you have heard about abductions, 221 persons were kidnapped and the fate of most of those remained unknown. Now, it is in the context of the KLA's existing behaviour towards Serb civilians or, as they termed them, colonizers, that the criminal motivation of those participating in the joint criminal enterprise in the Dukagjini area must be viewed. Now, what I wish to turn to before going into greater detail about the involvement of the three accused is the location of the mass grave along the canal. And we've printed out some copies of the large photographs of the canal which were marked by Professor Aleksandric, and perhaps if they could be distributed to the Trial Chamber and Defence counsel at the moment. The question that you must ask yourself is: Why did the KLA dump the bodies of its murder victims by this particular canal? Now, the canal area is too long to show in one photograph with any detail. The first photograph on the scene shows where the first group of bodies were located. The second photograph which shows the downstream area, shows where the other group of photographs were located. Now, if you ask yourself: Why did the KLA dump the bodies there? Why did the KLA just not bury them in a pit at Jablanica or Gllogjan? But if you examine the location and if you look at where it is and where it fits in, you'll see that it fits the classic picture of a mass execution or a mass grave site. The grave site was located far enough away from KLA focal points, such as the Haradinaj family compound, the Gllogjan KLA headquarters, the Black Eagles headquarters in Rznic, not to attract attention from international observers, but it was located deep within KLA-controlled territory. The area is a natural dumping-ground for bodies if you look at it. It's isolated. It's hard to get to. It would have been hard for the Serbian forces to get into it, and the evidence is they only got there in a very large joint military operation in a September, a joint MUP and VJ military operation. And importantly, it was near impossible for international monitors who were in the area, such as the ECMM, that's European Commission Monitoring Mission; the OSCE; or the Humanitarian Law Centre from Belgrade; or the British and American military attaches, such as Colonel Crosland who gave evidence here, it was near impossible for them to get into this area, guarded as it was by Balaj's Black Eagles training ground on one side and numerous KLA check-points, trenches and fortifications around the others. Now, it's also important to view the proximity of this particular location to the Haradinaj family compound. And if you look at the photograph on the screen now which we've also handed round, the line has been drawn which shows it is 1.94 kilometres in a straight line from the Haradinaj compound to the location, and that area, as I said before, was under KLA control. This was an area which one could not just stumble into. However, its existence was no secret at the time to those in the area, but nor could it be. Numerous people were aware of what was going on there. Now, turning to the joint criminal enterprise itself, the Prosecution has proved that between March and September 1998 in pursuing a common criminal purpose, Haradinaj, Balaj and Brahimaj and other KLA members acting pursuant to it created a "free zone," in the Dukagjini area, in which KLA forces could move and operate freely. It established a military structure under Haradinaj's ultimate military and civilian authority in that zone, and as I mentioned earlier conducted a campaign of violence and persecution against KLA opponents. Now, what was Ramush Haradinaj's role within the joint criminal enterprise and in pursuing the common criminal purpose? As the Trial Chamber has heard, Haradinaj is a strong, powerful, and charismatic individual. Some witnesses regarded him then, and still do, as an idol. One witness said there was an expression: God in heaven; Haradinaj on earth. He was a strong and dominant presence throughout the Dukagjini Zone throughout the indictment period. He was the KLA's military leader there and the most powerful individual in the indictment period in the Dukagjini Zone. He organized military operations, he commanded them, he controlled them, but also he took control of civilian affairs. Now, Haradinaj misused this position and he misused it to further the common criminal purpose. Haradinaj himself was instrumental in establishing, implementing, and maintaining the system of violence and persecution against perceived collaborators and KLA opponents in 1998. And without his participation, it could not have existed. His degree of control over both civilian and military matters in the zone in 1998 were such that the persecutions, the murders, tortures, abductions, rapes of Serb civilians and perceived opponents could not have occurred without his approval. The mistreatment and persecution was so widespread and so systematic that it could only have occurred with his approval. He established, supported, and was in overall command of the components, the main components of this system. The main structural instruments of this system included Balaj's Black Eagles, Brahimaj's detention centre, and the military police. But Haradinaj can exert at what can be described as a curious degree of power over both civilian and military matters. He moved constantly in the zone. He maintained extensive contact with KLA village commanders and other KLA officers. He engaged at a very detailed level in military matters. He himself personally ordered the assignment and transfer of individual soldiers and units, arming and weapons distributions, medical treatment, and the collection and distribution of supplies, military training, and the financing and distribution of funds. He personally approved weapons -- weapon-collecting trips to Albania and back. On the 24th of June, 1998, showing his power within the zone, Haradinaj ordered the mobilisation of all men aged between 19 and 35. The very minutes of that meeting prove his level of involvement in calling meetings, setting agendas, chairing them, issuing orders, receiving reports, controlling the discussion. The evidence proves that he had an exhaustively detailed knowledge of events and operations throughout that area. The evidence also proves that he led military operations throughout the area. The KLA subzone commander, Cufe Krasniqi, testified at page 5811 of this. Another commander, Shemsedin Cekaj also testified of how Haradinaj was often at the front lines. His degree of military involvement and control is shown by the fact that he hand-selected his commanders in the area. He appointed Balaj, as I've said before, to command the Black Eagles; Rrustem Tetaj and Shemsedin Cekaj as village commanders; Din Krasniqi, and that's an important name in this case as the commander of Baran valley; Faton Mehmetaj, a name I'll return to later as a commander of the military police; Nazmi Brahimaj as the deputy; and another name I'll return to later, Pjeter Shala as the commander of Dujak, he appointed him on the 2nd of July. Haradinaj had extensive contact with Din Krasniqi in Vranoc. Krasniqi reported to Haradinaj and took orders from him. Pjeter Shala testified of Haradinaj's personal authorisations. He said: "I don't know the exact time, but I went to Gllogjan for every piece of document that I needed." That's at page 9980. Another example which is Exhibit P1266 is of Haradinaj's signing KLA registration certificates. This one on the screen now in Albanian showing his signature, and in English, shows him issuing a certificate to a businessman from Pristina, Shefqet Cemaj [phoen] on the 4th of July and having them issued with two bombs. The briefs at paragraph 156 sets out how Haradinaj warned and dismissed subordinates at the least sign of disloyalty, including the proposed expulsion of Nazmi Brahimaj [sic] for having committing an "act of treason" by leaving his post contrary to Haradinaj's instructions. The level of control exercised by Haradinaj also necessary for him to participate in the joint criminal enterprise is also shown by the way he gave himself ultimate civilian authority in that zone in the indictment period. Documents tendered into evidence prove that Ramush Haradinaj personally controlled matters such as health care, registration of births and deaths, vehicle registration, travel permits and civilian movement, and he even controlled woodcutting, personally issuing permits allowing individuals to cut wood. On the 22nd of July, he went so far as to forbid anyone in that area from consuming or selling alcoholic beverages. Such was his degree of control over all matters civilian and military that he prohibited not just the military but civilians from consuming and selling alcohol, that's Exhibit P246. Haradinaj also established KLA control over the movement of the civilian population with a -- with an intricate system of village check-points. Travel authorisations were issued by KLA village commanders, who of course reported to Haradinaj. Exhibit P146 demonstrates how on the 24th of June Haradinaj expressly issued an order in which he expressly prohibited the movement of the civilian population without permission from the relevant KLA headquarters. Paragraph 7 of that reads, and it's on the screen: "The movement of the combatants, military officers, and the population within the region of responsibility of the Operational Headquarters of the Plain of Dukagjinit is prohibited without the permission of the command of the relevant headquarters." On July 9th, 1998, at a work meeting of his own staff, and again proving the level of interest shown by Haradinaj in the movement of civilians within his zone, he emphasised that permits should be issued only for one trip to one village. Now, a sinister reason, the evidence has proved, existed for this degree of interest in the movements of civilians, one trip to one village and so on, because controlling the movement of civilians in this manner allowed the KLA to easily locate and detain perceived collaborators and KLA opponents, which was part of the common criminal purpose of the joint criminal enterprise. Now, this is directly proved by the number of victims in this indictment, of which you've heard much evidence, who were taken into custody at KLA check-points, they include in Counts 5 and 6, Stanisa and Rosa Radosevic and Novak Stijovic; in Counts 17 and 18, Tush and Illira Frrokaj; Counts 21 and 22, Sanije Balaj and Sejd Noci; Counts 27 and 28, Witness 6; and in Counts 29 and 30, Nenad Remistar. On the 2nd of July, Exhibit P158, Haradinaj went so far as to ban political parties or organizations. Now, the order you can see on the screen in front of you is headed: "Executive Order." And it says: "It is banned any political activity from any political party or association of a political nature in the Operational Zone of Dukagjini Plain. We order the abolition of political parties until the full liberation of the country." As you can see in the Albanian the order is issued and bears Haradinaj's signature. Another example of Haradinaj's interest in civilian matters is an order issued on the 28th of July authorising Fadil and Bekim Betiki [phoen] - sorry, if I pronounced that wrongly - to supply foodstuffs in that area, salt, sugar, oil, and pasta. In that order Haradinaj is authorising who can supply normal foodstuffs to the population in the Dukagjini area. A handwritten note which is an order which is Exhibit P127, signed by Nazim and -- Nazmi Brahimaj and Ramush Haradinaj simply refers to the transfer of one Fadil on the 9th of June, 1998, from dispensary facilities to one for better facilities. The purpose of showing this one is to demonstrate the degree of interest that Haradinaj and others accused in participating in the joint criminal enterprise showed in the minutia of life in the Dukagjini Zone in July 1998. Another thing shows his control, influence, command, control, and authority is the detention on the 11th of August, 1998, of the ECMM monitor, Achilleas Pappas. On that date, Idriz Balaj stopped and detained him and several other ECMM monitors, accusing him of being a Serbian spy. Balaj took Pappas' group of suspected spies to the Gllogjan headquarters. There Balaj, himself, personally beat this Greek air force captain and international monitor's Albanian interpreter, no doubt because of his involvement or association with a suspected Serbian spy, albeit one with diplomatic immunity. Pappas testified that: "Balaj started beating and kicking the interpreter, calling him names, and making some gestures like he was trying to get the gun from his waistcoat and shoot him." Now, after that Haradinaj arrived and interrogated the members of the group before allowing them to leave. Pappas in his statement before this court Exhibit P271 at paragraph 26, described those who detained him and the monitors as extremists, that was the third group of KLA people he had met in Kosovo and here he refers to: "The group that abducted us." He said: "They acted separately within a certain area, which they had totally under their control. They had their leader, whom they were following in an obedient manner, without questioning his person or orders. By saying this, I refer to the person of Ramush Haradinaj. Before Haradinaj appeared, the other soldiers were rude and behaving in a bad way. Once he appeared, they started to calm down and behaved in a more normal way. I point out, however, that I only saw Ramush Haradinaj issue an order twice. The first order was given when he was searching the car and a group of soldiers, including a woman, arrived and saluted him." Going down: "The second was when he ordered the three black uniformed men who had abducted us, including Idriz Balaj, to escort us away." Now, fundamental to Haradinaj's control of the zone and the implementation of the common criminal purpose was his deliberate - and I emphasise deliberate - neglect of internal KLA discipline in relation to the known crimes committed against civilians. During the indictment period he established no system, absolutely no system, of military courts or internal discipline; rather, he used the military police to further the common criminal purpose. Haradinaj allowed his subordinates within the KLA to operate throughout the indictment period with impunity from prosecution or discipline throughout that time and throughout that zone. It is important that not one of the 14 officer positions in his staff related to military discipline. An experienced former JNA officer, Rrustem Tetaj even testified that he was unaware of any military disciplinary measures taken against any KLA member in that area between May and September 1998. In fact, the evidence proves that the only disciplinary measures that appear to have been taken relate to acts of disloyalty. The evidence proves overwhelmingly that Haradinaj took no measures against the KLA members who committed the numerous crimes against civilians pleaded in the indictment and proved at trial. Now, in the Prosecution's submission, this was not accidental, it was entirely deliberate. Haradinaj had near absolute authority in the zone where the crimes were being committed. Had he so wanted to, he could have dismissed or otherwise disciplined KLA members committing these numerous and known crimes against the civilian population. Rather, he chose deliberately to further the common purpose, the common criminal purpose, by permitting and encouraging KLA members to commit these crimes. In fact, the only system of "discipline" implemented by Haradinaj was the system of violence and persecution imposed against civilians and civilians who were perceived as collaborators. The focus of the KLA command in imposing what it called "disciplinary measures" for perceived anti-KLA activity is in fact illustrated by the minutes of the meeting of the Dukagjini staff held on the 24th of June, and the evidence proves that Haradinaj never investigated or punished the notorious disappearances in his area of control. For example, the case of Witness 6, who was imprisoned and tortured in the Jablanica detention centre in June 1998 provides a clear example of how it operated in practice. After six weeks of detention and torture, Nazmi Brahimaj eventually released this prisoner by giving him a release permit saying that pursuant to KLA regulations, this is Exhibit P355, the staff, operative staff, has decided that the accused, that is Witness 6, shall be released. His release is conditional; if he repeats his mistake, he will be prosecuted. The KLA military police service was absolutely integral to the joint criminal enterprise. Now, unlike any normal military police service, the role of this police service, rather than being there -- rather than existing to enforce military discipline, existed to hunt down its suspected or the KLA-suspected opponents. The evidence has proved conclusively that Haradinaj had a close working relationship with the military police and the military police could not have committed the crimes without his imprimatur. Haradinaj even proposed its governing regulations. Exhibit P140 shows the regulations of 3 and 4 showing that it had the task of "investigating and in uncovering with persuasive facts all those persons who collaborate in any way with the enemy." Regulation 4 said: "The military police is obliged to take measures against all those working against the KLA." Haradinaj appointed his loyal subordinate, a name I mentioned before, Faton Mehmetaj, as its commander. Rrustem Tetaj, a KLA sub-commander explained to the Chamber that Mehmetaj black-listed people who were suspected of being disloyal to the KLA, sympathizing with the opposition LDK or having worked with the MUP or other authorities and Mehmetaj circulated this black list amongst KLA village guards. Now, these were guards who operated the system of check-points in controlling the movement of the civilian population. The evidence has proved that the KLA military police detained and mistreated and/or murdered at least five victims in the indictment, Kemal Gashi, Zenun Gashi, Sanije Balaj, Naser Lika and Fadil Fazliu, all for their alleged collaboration or opposition to the KLA. Each of these victims shared the characteristics which illustrate the nature of Haradinaj's system of persecution. None was a KLA member. Each was alleged to be a collaborator or KLA opponent. The three who were murdered after detention by the KLA military police were last seen alive around Baran. Each of their bodies, that's R-1, 2, and 4, which should be displayed on the screen now, were disposed of approximately 10 kilometres away in the same group of bodies found in the canal in September 1998. Now, while of course all of this was occurring, KLA military police were detaining, abducting, mistreating, and even murdering opponents of the KLA, Haradinaj was reporting to the General Staff in Exhibit P224 that, it's coming up on the screen: "We have formed the military police and it is functioning well." We will find that exhibit in a moment, it's 224 and it's the last page in the English. I repeat those words. At the time this was occurring Haradinaj was reporting to the General Staff of the KLA: "We have formed the military police and it is functioning well." Well, for the purposes of the common criminal purpose of the joint criminal enterprise it was doing its job very, very well, as the evidence has established. Several days later, on the 1st of August, 1998, Haradinaj ordered all local headquarters of the Dukagjini Zone to assist this very same military police which was doing its job so well. And you can see the list of duties, one of which is: "To act against the enemy in response to the needs of the front lines." The other one is: "To assist the military police." By that order, Haradinaj was encouraging KLA local staff to assist the military police in carrying out its function, its part of the common criminal purpose of the joint criminal enterprise. As mentioned before to implement the common criminal purpose of the joint criminal enterprise Haradinaj needed to eliminate opposition to his forces within the Dukagjini Zone. Now, the brief also describes in detail the conflict between the armed forces of Kosovo, that's the FARK, and the KLA when FARK soldiers crossed from Albania into Haradinaj's zone in June -- in late June, 1998, that's at paragraphs 156 through to 167. As mentioned, the common criminal purpose required his control over the zone and the crushing of any opposition. And the more moderate an opposition supporting FARK represented a potential threat to Haradinaj and his control over the zone. And it was during the period that the FARK were in his zone between June and August 1998 that Haradinaj and other participants in the joint criminal enterprise continued with their persecution of perceived collaborators and civilian opponents of the KLA, imprisoning them and torturing them at Jablanica, circulating wanted lists of collaborators, some of whom of course ended up buried by the canal. Now, Haradinaj and Balaj's personal confrontation with FARK soldiers on the 4th of July is illustrative of how they, that is, Haradinaj, Balaj, and other members of the joint criminal enterprise, dealt with this potential threat posed by FARK to their common criminal purpose. Their expressed view was: The FARK forces had to leave. Now, FARK soldier, Witness 29, testified about the attitude of Haradinaj's KLA soldiers to the FARK. He said at page 3499: " ... I was told that if we did not go back to Albania, Mr. Haradinaj, together with his officers and soldiers under his command, would fight us first and then the -- sorry, would fight us first and then the Serb forces. By this I mean they would kill us all first and then fight the enemy." He went on at page 3496 and he said: " ... During the meeting between Mr. Haradinaj and Mr. Tahir Zemaj," that's the FARK commander, we've heard a lot of evidence about the confrontation or the involvement between Tahir Zemaj and Haradinaj, "what was said was that, You don't need to come to Kosova. You have to go back where you came from. Kosova doesn't need you. Kosova doesn't need the armed forces of the Republic of Kosovo or FARK. If you don't go back, we will fight you. We will not fight the enemy. We will leave the enemy, and we will fight you." But it goes on. On the 4th of July, Witness 29 and three other FARK soldiers were forcibly abducted by Idriz Balaj and Ramush Haradinaj's brother Daut Haradinaj and taken to Gllogjan, where they met Ramush himself. After what was described as an initially warm reception Haradinaj pistol-whipped one of the FARK soldiers and then led a brutal beating of the four men by a group of between 20 to 30 KLA soldiers. The Trial Chamber heard evidence from Witness 29 that during the beating Haradinaj personally shot the witness in the right shoulder. The Witness testified at page 53 -- sorry, 3530 in relation to Haradinaj trying to shoot him in the neck. "He wanted to hit me on the neck, but because of the movement that I was doing at the time, the bullet hit my arm and not on the neck where he wanted to hit me." Witness 29 continued -- after his beating finished he was asked: "Now, how long did the beating last?" He said he couldn't say. "It started suddenly. It ended suddenly ... So both the starting moment and the ending moment were sudden." But then he said after the beating finished this is what he saw: "At that time, I saw they were dragging the other soldiers by their hair. Daut Haradinaj and Idriz Balaj were dragging them by their hair and beating them at the same time. They were dragging them towards the village of Gllogjan." And further at page 3531 after the attack stopped suddenly he said, that's at line 14: "When the attack stopped, I saw Idriz, Petrit, and Azem being dragged by their hair by Daut and Balaj who had been beaten with Kalashnikovs and with the butts of the pistols, also punching and so on. They were dragging them towards the headquarters." "And where was Ramush?" "At that time," said Witness 29, "Ramush still had his pistol in his hand. He kept that in his hand all the time and he said to me: 'You only got two minutes to leave the village of Gllogjan. And walk straight, straight along the main road. You've only got two minutes to leave the village.' While the other soldiers were taken into the headquarters of the Gllogjan village which was Haradinaj's headquarters."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, since you are not having your earphones on, you got a message from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will slow down. I apologise. Tahir Zemaj himself reported the attack to the Supreme Command on the 5th of July in Exhibit P167. Now, what was Haradinaj's personal participation proved at trial? The evidence has proved that Haradinaj misused most egregiously his position of command. It could be described as setting a tone of acceptable violence in the Dukagjin area; however, the tone he set was very loud or very high. He took personal acts of violence against those he perceived as opposing the KLA as I've just described with the FARK soldiers. The acts proved with brutal -- these acts proved with brutal clarity his approval and encouragement of the elimination and perceived opposition by his subordinates through fear and violence. He, Haradinaj, could not have sent a clearer message to his subordinates within the KLA and to the civilian population. One example is his personal participation in the attack by his KLA subordinates on his Serbian neighbours and their cousins -- and their cousin, sorry, on the 18th of April, 1998, which is charged in Counts 3 and 4. The evidence has proved that by Orthodox Easter 1998, virtually no Serb families remained in the Gllogjan area, and it's also proved that Ramush Haradinaj took his own personal steps to ensure that this was the case. He took personal steps to mistreat and to expel his own Serb neighbours from Dubrave which is right next to his house, family compound, in Gllogjan. Your Honours heard the evidence that Haradinaj had lived next to Dragoslav Stojanovic a mere two years older than Haradinaj. They had walked to school together, they grew up together next door to each other, they knew each other well. What happened? On the 18th of April, 1998, soldiers, KLA soldiers under Haradinaj's command, abducted, persecuted, and tortured his neighbours, Dragoslav and Mijat Stojanovic and their cousin, Veselin Stijovic, who were all Serb civilians. After that, they were forcibly transferred from -- Stojanovic was forcibly transferred from their home to Serb-controlled territory outside the Dukagjini zone. Now, Dragoslav Stojanovic gave chilling testimony of Haradinaj's personal presence in Gllogjan on that day. The evidence establishes that about 30 KLA soldiers, including again Haradinaj's brother Daut, had entered and searched the Stojanovic's house. They then forced three men to lie face down on the floor and cursing their ethnicity kicked and beat them with rifle-butts. The beating continued outside until Nasim Haradinaj arrived and ordered them taken to KLA headquarters in Gllogjan. Bleeding and seriously injured, the three were forced to walk to the KLA headquarters in Smajl Haradinaj's house in Gllogjan about 1500 metres away. KLA soldiers beat and insulted them along the way, saying that all Serbs should leave Kosovo. This is of course consistent with the content of the KLA communiques, as shown before. Haradinaj was standing nearby. He was personally present, and he must have seen the large group of armed KLA soldiers forcing these three Serb civilians down the road in broad daylight while beating them and cursing at them. His brother Daut and two other KLA soldiers took these three victims to the upper floor of the headquarters and accused them - and this is the common theme throughout this case - of spying for the Serbs. Now, of Ramush Haradinaj's personal presence and involvement there, his neighbour, Dragoslav Stojanovic, testified at page 1886. "You've just mentioned Ramush, did you see him at all there? "A. Yes, but not in that room. Ramush came by later in the course of that day with five or six other soldiers accompanying him. I was lying on the floor in that corridor, since I was unable to move. I wasn't allowed to move either. He came by with five or six of his soldiers, they were his escort, I suppose, I don't know. He came in, shoved me with his leg, and said, Hello neighbour, do you recognise me? I said, No, I don't, and then he kicked me in the back saying that I would eventually learn who he was." Next question: "How hard did he kick you? "A. Well," he said, "it seemed hard enough to me. At the time it certainly felt hard enough since he was wearing those military boots." That's displayed on the screen at the moment. Now, of course Dragoslav Stojanovic knew exactly who Haradinaj was and he had very, very good personal reasons for not admitting it in that moment of fear in the state he was in. At page 1888 to 9, he told the Trial Chamber when asked: "Did you in fact recognise him when he came in? Answer was: "Yes, yes, I knew him well. "Q. Why did you say, No, I don't recognise you, when he asked you if you did? "A. Because virtually we were one of the first to be arrested and captured in the area. It was for fear of saying that I knew him. It was for fear of getting killed, otherwise one of us could later have gone on to the police and told them about it or something. One thing I must say, he wasn't the only one to ask me at the time. His brother -- his cousins came over, too, Padram, Smajl's son ... Came to ask me, Neighbour, do you recognise me? I didn't answer any of them ... I said no to each and every one of them. "And then the son of Mustafa, he had been abroad quite a long time, he came over that day and asked me the same question. I gave the same answer to everyone, No, I don't know you." The Trial Chamber has to ask itself what else could Mr. Stojanovic have done in those circumstances. Fearing for his life, he felt the only thing he could do to protect himself was to deny knowledge of his long-time neighbour, Ramush Haradinaj. But Haradinaj's words are chilling in the context of what occurred in this case because it showed his recognition of who was now in control, who was responsible for expelling the Serbs, who controlled and commanded that area. We, the KLA, are now in control; you, Serb civilians, are out. And his words there are entirely consistent with the evidence you have heard of the mistreatment, persecution, and targeting of Serb civilians in the early status of the indictment period. Now, what of his injuries? Of his injuries Dragoslav Stojanovic testified at page 1889 that he was severely injured. He said: "In addition to having blood on my face from the beatings, I didn't have any open wounds. As for my internal injuries, my pancreas was ruptured, my stomach in two different places, the colon, the stomach walls were crushed. You might say large-scale internal injuries, a whole lot of pain, enormous pain, and this feeling of suffocation." When asked: "Had you already sustained those injuries at the point when Haradinaj kicked you, or did you sustain those injuries later, or you can't say?" He answered: "It must have been before." The evidence proves that Haradinaj seeing his brutalized and seriously injured neighbour lying on the floor in KLA captivity in KLA headquarters in Gllogjan brutalized him further by kicking a defenceless man who claimed not to know who Haradinaj was. The "Spotlight" report of the Humanitarian Law Centre, that's Exhibit P6, also refers to this incident which was well-known at the time. I take you to paragraph 9.1 where you can see there's an extract saying that: "Dragoslav and Mijat Stojanovic and their son [sic] Veselin -- were seized by uniformed men and taken to headquarters in Gllogjan and it has the testimony given to the HLC at the time of Mijat Stojanovic at the time. The meaning of Haradinaj's words to his seriously injured neighbour became clear over the ensuing days as the KLA violently expelled and murdered the few Serbs who still remained in the villages around Gllogjan. And the evidence has proved that by the 23rd of April, five days after Haradinaj, his brother Daut, and other KLA subordinates mistreated so badly the Stojanovic brothers, his neighbours, and expelled them from the house, the KLA had expelled virtually all remaining Serbs from the villages around Gllogjan. Several of them were detained and then taken to Gllogjan for beating or interrogation before being expelled, Novak Stijovic and Stanisa Radosevic are examples. And the KLA as the evidence proves murdered the few who stayed behind. These include sisters Vukosava Markovic and Darinka Kovac, and Milovan and Milka Vlahovic, Slobodan Radosevic and Milos Radunovic. After KLA members helped one Serb family and its Serb neighbours flee Dashinoc on the 23rd of April, Haradinaj showed his personally disapproval of allowing that Serbian family to leave. The Trial Chamber heard testimony that Haradinaj went to the village and publicly castigated a KLA member demanding to know why he had allowed the families to leave the village unharmed.

utterances.text: There's a -- thank you, Your Honour, there's a small correction to the transcript at page 18, line 14, it says Nasim not Nazmi, if that could be corrected or the other way around. Now, consistent with KLA communiques 13, 18, and 23, all in evidence, that describe Serbs as "colonizers," the opinion of the KLA members about the presence of Montenegrins in the KLA "free zone" is shown by these minutes which record the Dobrigje representative reporting to the meeting. The minutes show or give evidence of the persecutory intent of those present at the meeting, including Ramush Haradinaj. Referring to the situation and for no other reason, I submit, other than ethnic reasons which go to the mens rea of persecution. The minutes record the Dobrigje representative saying: "We have two Montenegrin houses, ten people. We are able to resort to weapons." Now, what could that mean? In the context of the evidence the Trial Chamber has heard about attacks upon Serb and Montenegrin civilians and perceived collaborators, other than that these people were now under direct threat by virtue only of their ethnicity by the KLA. And in fact, it is no coincidence that within days the KLA had attacked these Montenegrin families in Dobrigje and had abducted a Serb civilian, Zdravko Radunovic who made the mistake of travelling to see these Montenegrin relatives there. His body was found at the canal in September 1998. Also on the issue of ethnic slurs which goes to persecutory intention, Stanisa Radosevic testified of ethnic slurs he received from KLA soldiers while they were beating him, this is at page 973 of the transcript. He said: "They," that is, the KLA soldiers, "cursed our Serbian mothers, asking us, "What do you want? Do you know who we are? They told us all sorts of things. At page 974, consistent with the KLA modus operandi of those acting pursuant to the common criminal purpose, he said of the beating: "When I tried to protect Novak, he hit me with their fists," that's a KLA soldier, "until I fell down, then they kicked me while I was down. When I came around, they threw us on to the car, and they continued kicking us and also using rifle-butts to hit us. I also received a blow with a pistol butt on the head and my hand was bleeding." They wanted to know everything about these people." Again, when viewed in the historical context of KLA communiques describing -- sorry, these must be viewed in the historical context of the KLA communiques describing Serbs as colonizers in terms of the persecution that occurred. As another example --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I move to the area of the topic of Haradinaj's and the KLA's control over the free zone in the Dukagjini area. Now, the brief in some detail in paragraphs 76 to 95 describes the creation of the KLA free zone and its boundaries. As the Court heard, the evidence was more or less consistent between Defence -- I'm sorry, between Serbian civilian and KLA witnesses as to the area which the KLA controlled and when it controlled it within the indictment period. Now, I've mentioned earlier that the KLA fighters maintained security in their free zone through check-points and observation posts. And the KLA fighters were able to move about that zone freely and openly. The extent of these zones or these check-points is shown by the testimony of one KLA member, Shaban Balaj, who testified that: "Almost every village within the area north and west of Lake Radoniq had a KLA check-point up until September 1998." Now, both KLA and international witnesses passed through numerous check-points within the zone. You've heard testimony that some of these check-points so close were the sides to each other at times were only 50 metres from the Peje-Gjakove road, and it was through these check-points that the KLA controlled access to the Dukagjini zone. You've heard testimony from witnesses who described the check-points as routine and normal in that area. You've heard evidence of KLA village commanders issuing travel permits to civilians to allow them to pass through these check-points. But in the transcript and at trial a consistent answer emerged to questions about Haradinaj's control over this area. For example, British military attache, Colonel John Crosland, who was very used to assessing those sorts of areas, that was one of the reasons he travelled from Belgrade to Kosovo frequently, it was to assess the strength of the KLA and Serbian forces and to monitor the situation, he met Haradinaj personally in March or April 1998. And he testified of Haradinaj's control at that point. As you can see on the screen, it says: "Q. What was your understanding about the extent of Haradinaj's control or command when you met him?" And he answered: "I think I'm right in saying he indicated that he controlled what was called the Dukagjin area, which is the area I'd explained and the importance of that area. And this was, I think, alluded to or confirmed, whichever way you want to, in his assessment which had been made by outside intelligence agencies." Now, as I mentioned a moment ago, Crosland was well-placed to make that assessment himself. Haradinaj was making the assessment, Crosland was making the assessment, and it coincided with what the intelligence sources were telling them. Now, that also coincided with Witness 29's testimony, at page 3488. The question was: "During this time-period, between March 24 and late June 1998, in your discussions with KLA soldiers and village commanders, did you learn if there was a KLA overall commander for the Dukagjini Zone?" And he went on, I take you to the second line of the passage, where it says: "Not the entire Dukagjini Zone was in a state of war," he says: "But each and every one were saying that Ramush Haradinaj was the overall commander." Now, during this trial, the Presiding Judge, Judge Orie, asked Colonel Crosland some very pertinent questions about the KLA command and control, and Crosland testified at 3029, and it's on the screen now, about the respective positions. "The Serbs, likewise, took up the position that they could, if you like, contain the fighters within this area by dominating the roads. I don't agree with the strategy, but that was the way they did it. "So the area remained -- the Serbian security forces would go off the road a short way, make a raid, re-arrange a few houses rather badly, and then withdraw back out because they didn't feel safe in the area. Now, that was their way of dealing with localised incidents that happened in and around these major proceeds from Pec to Klina down to Djakovica and back up to Pec. So the roads provided the access, and not often -- I mean, one of the major incidents was going -- the Serbs -- we were asked to go with the Serbs to visit this supposed massacre site at Gllogjan, beyond Gllogjan, on the water area" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
