utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He went on: "Now, I don't think many of them went further than, say, 5 or 6 kilometres off the road because they were going into a territory that they really were not familiar with. So that is why I've said that the area, in my opinion, and it is only my opinion, was basically a KLA area and the Serbs would stay on the outside and attempt to dominate and influence areas by shelling into the area" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "Long-range indirect fire by tanks or by armoured personnel carriers or anti-aircraft vehicles." Now, Defence counsel Mr. Emmerson put the question fairly and squarely to KLA sub-zone commander to Shemsedin Cekaj at page 4486. Mr. Emmerson's question was: "So, Mr. Cekaj ... I'm suggesting to you that between" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re. Mr. Re, if you would slow down not just for a second but slow down more permanently than the -- certainly the French translation would be able to follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "I'm suggesting to you that between the 26th of May, when you arrived and the 12th of July when you left, there were Serb forces, including paramilitaries, operating from time to time in the territory along the canal?" Completely dispelling this, Cekaj answered: "I have no information about that. It was impossible for the Serbian forces to enter there at that time." Now, the importance of Gllogjan and control over that area for both the common criminal purposes and the military purposes is shown by Mr. Stijovic's statement at paragraph 25 where he said: "The KLA organized the receipt and distribution of the equipment throughout Kosovo and Metohija using the already established channels. Gllogjan and Jablanica were strategically located on that route and, for this reason, the Haradinaj family later assumed an important position within the KLA. They had the ability to decide who was allowed to travel through their area and who was not. KLA commanders from other areas had to seek permission for their men to travel through this area on their way to and from the Albanian border. The villages of Jablanica and Gllogjan became KLA logistics bases of a sort, controlled by the Brahimaj and Haradinaj families respectively." At paragraph 61 of his statement, he gives further insight into what was occurring there where he said: "As a result of these territorial advances in April, May, and June, the KLA succeeded to a significant degree in creating a single 'free zone' linking Drenica, Dukagjin, and the Albanian border. The Albanian strongholds in the villages of Gllogjan, Jablanica, Junik, Jasic, and Smonica had a special strategic importance in this regard. Our sources indicated that most KLA weapons came from Albania, either through black markets overseas, or from Bosnia and Croatia. These weapons were mainly of Chinese or Yugoslav origin at the outset, but the KLA came to have the most modern 'Armbrust' rocket-launchers used by the NATO." In relation to the strength or the intensity of the armed conflict, the Trial Chamber heard a lot of evidence from KLA fighters, international observers and you heard evidence from two Serbian retired generals. I'll just take you briefly to the evidence of Mr. Stijovic in relation to the weapons flowing into Albania where he said at page 9010: "This is an official UN report from the summer of 1997 - that over 650.000 pieces of weapons, a vast quantity of weapons disappeared from official military depots in Albania. All measures taken by official Albanian authorities later, with the help of the international community, led to an estimate by the UN commission that 30 to 40 per cent of these weapons were not under the control of the authorities and the bulk of this quantity, 30 to 40 per cent out of 650.000 pieces, ended up in the possession of the KLA." In giving the KLA a bit of a back-handed compliment he added: "The KLA used this situation in the best way possible. I have to grant them that." As an example of the sophistication of the KLA weapons, arming, and fortifications, I just briefly have displayed Exhibit P910 which are photographs of KLA trenches, fortifications, and positions at Lodza when the Serbs overran the position in July 1998. Colonel or retired General Dragan Zivanovic in testimony in his statement under Rule 92 ter, P1018, at paragraphs 103 to 104 displayed on the screen also paid the KLA some compliments in terms of the resistance he encountered. In describing fighting in Prilep in August 1998, he described: "We encountered very strong resistance from the KLA. KLA fighters were using the stone towers in the walled and enclosed family compounds to shoot at the MUP and VJ. These towers were very suitable for sniping at our forces. The sound made by the Chinese automatic rifles also made it very difficult to ascertain the firing positions."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "The KLA were firing at us from behind the stone walls ... Using hand-held rocket-launchers. The courtyard in the centre of the village was particularly difficult for us to take because the KLA was firing a mortar at us from that position. I know all the civilians ... Left the village before the MUP and VJ entered Prilep and the fighting began." Then he goes on: "We were unable to use tanks ... Because the terrain was flat and we could not find a direct line of sight on targets." And he then said: "As our units approached their stone buildings they managed to escape through holes dug under the stone walls. The KLA also mined the houses and buildings and parts of the courtyards with personnel mines and ... Explosive devices."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I turn now to the role of Idriz Balaj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sorry. To the role of Idriz Balaj, also known as Toger, and the Black Eagles. The evidence has proved beyond any reasonable doubt that Idriz Balaj is and was Toger. No one has suggested in the Defence that there was more than one Toger operating in the Dukagjini Zone in 1998, nor that another Toger, a different Toger to Idriz Balaj, ran the Black Eagles, a unit notorious for its brutality towards Serbs and perceived civilian opponents of the KLA. Balaj commanded the Black Eagles; Haradinaj appointed him to that position in 1998. They had a particularly close working relationship. Balaj was an important member of Haradinaj's Gllogjan staff. Balaj, Toger, acted as Haradinaj's personal body-guard. They were frequently seen together. Balaj accompanied Haradinaj to almost every important KLA/FARK meeting in the Dukagjini Zone. At those meetings between FARK and the KLA, Balaj was responsible for Haradinaj's security. His position was formalised or set out in Exhibit P177, which shows the composition of the Gllogjan staff as of the 8th of July, 1998, and you can see at item 11, which is displayed on the screen -- or the whole thing, you can see that Togeri, that is, Balaj, was the commander of the special units. You can also see other familiar names, Faton Mehmetaj in Poxha [phoen], Daut Haradinaj, Shkelzen Haradinaj, Ramush Haradinaj as the commander. The minutes of the meeting of the 23rd of June, 1998, that's Exhibit 143, reveal Balaj's position to be "responsible for sabotage and anti-terrorist combat." Togeri and it says: "Decision." And you can see the Albanian on the screen and it's about the middle of the page. However described, in reality, however, his task was to locate, mistreat, and murder alleged collaborators and KLA opponents in furtherance of the common criminal purpose. The Black Eagles wore distinctive uniforms, they were better armed than normal KLA soldiers, they were better trained, they were based in the Gllogjan elementary school until Balaj, Toger, moved it to Rznic after the MUP withdrew after the 21st of April. Balaj himself, and there's been an amount of evidence about this, drove a distinctive black jeep. The Black Eagles operated with impunity throughout the Dukagjini area. They trained at the abandoned Ekonomija farm, a state agricultural enterprise which was directly next to the canal where the 31 bodies were found. Its location could be seen on the photograph directly in front of the Trial Chamber at the moment. Balaj and the Black Eagles entered villages looking for people who were "wanted" by the KLA. Balaj kept a notebook containing names of wanted persons. Two examples are civilians Faik Gecaj and Musa Berisha. A KLA commander or sub-commander Rrustem Tetaj testified that Faik Gecaj was on the list because he had been smuggling weapons from Albania for personal gain, but Musa Berisha worked for a human rights organization in Decan. Until 1998 -- sorry, the Trial Chamber heard evidence that in June 1998 Balaj shot at Musa Berisha's car at a check-point in Rznic when Berisha, an unarmed civilian, was attempting to reach Gllogjan. You also heard evidence of Balaj shooting an elderly civilian, Adem Hulaj, in Rznic as he was exiting his car. Balaj also led KLA members in brutally and repeatedly harassing and abducting and ultimately murdering three members of Witness 4's family because of Witness 4's family connections or alleged connections with Serbian authorities. Balaj abducted and mistreated Witness 1 based on suspected collaboration. He took Sanije Balaj's body to the canal area. He dumped it directly on the top of the mother of Witness 4 and her daughter who he had abducted some months earlier. He also personally committed the rapes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He also personally committed the rape charged in Counts 35, 36 and 37 of the indictment. Balaj was also involved in further violent and threatening acts, for example, and I've described these -- I've touched on these earlier: His and Haradinaj's mistreatment, intimidation of FARK soldiers and officers on 4th of July. In early July he attempted to intimidate a senior FARK officer in Rznic by questioning the officer's authority to travel in the area. And as described earlier, the detention on the 11th of August of the ECMM monitors in Rznic accusing them of spying for the Serbs and beating their Albanian interpreter. The evidence was that even KLA members feared Balaj. Pjeter Shala, himself a feared participant in the joint criminal enterprise, testified that other units "did not meddle" with Toger's unit. Avni Krasniqi, the KLA military police member, testified that when he went with Balaj and two other soldiers to move Sanije Balaj's body, he took another KLA soldier with him, such was his fear of Toger whom he identified as Idriz Balaj. Pjeter Shala testified of the security at Balaj's training facility, that's at pages 9974 to 5, and how Haradinaj's permission was required to visit it. And this is certainly something Shala should know about. "Q. And ... Was it easy to visit the location or base of ... This elite unit or special ... Unit? "A. I didn't have anything to do with that unit, but to go there you had to ask for special permission because other units didn't meddle with that unit. "Q. And do you know from whom ... You had to get that special authorisation? "A. From Ramush." It was well-known within the FARK that Balaj was abducting civilians. Witness 17 testified at page 7579 to 80 that Tahir Zemaj had said that if someone was detained and sent -- or taken to Gllogjan and his whereabouts are unknown, then it is Toger's responsibility who carried out these detentions. And that's why the villagers were interested in these things and provided Tahir with information on these incidents, since something was wrong. It was said that the missing persons, those that were detained and who went missing ... They were "sent to Gllogjan." Witness 4 lost his mother and two sisters to Balaj's persecution of them because of the family's alleged involvement with Serbian authorities. He testified about what his sister had said. "Q. What did she tell you? "A. She said that there was a prison in Irzniq. "Q. Who was this prison run by? "A. The KLA. "Q. Did your sister tell you anything about what she saw in this prison in Rznic? "A. ... She said she saw some prisoners of young and old in age. "Q. Did she tell you anything about what she had done or what the orders were in general as a member of the KLA? "A. Yes. She talked to us. She said that she had received orders from Togeri," that's Balaj, "to kill somebody and then if she didn't kill him, then he would kill me." In our brief we have given a table listing the sightings of Idriz Balaj throughout the indictment period. I want to show that table in PowerPoint, which shows Idriz Balaj's sightings throughout the period. If that could please be displayed. The first page it refers to paragraph 253 of the final trial brief. First sighting is training KLA soldiers in March 1998. Next, late March 1998, attending the funeral of KLA soldiers in Gllogjan. The third, formation and training of the Black Eagles in Gllogjan, April/May. Meeting Tetaj with Haradinaj, mid-April. Abducting Sister S, mid-April. Returning Sister S home, mid-April. Meeting Shemsedin Cekaj, 20th of April, and that was with Haradinaj. Driving his black jeep in Lumbardh, May 1998. Returning Sister S home a second time, early May 1998. Issuing a travel warning to Witness 4's family, that's late May 1998. June 1998, shooting Adem Hulaj as I described a moments ago. June 1998 shooting Musa Berisha in Rznic -- sorry, the car. Next one, taking Besim from Irzniq to dig trenches in June 1998. June 1998, again abducting Witness 4's family in Ratis -- mother in Ratis. 26th of June 1998, FARK/KLA meeting, Haradinaj attended in Jasic. 4th of July, confrontation with FARK soldiers. 4th of July, attacking FARK soldiers in Gllogjan in the presence of Haradinaj. 8th of July, the confrontation Witness 17 testified to in Irzniq. 10th of July, again with Haradinaj, delivering an ultimatum to the FARK command in Prapaqan. 10th/11th of July, Witness 17 complained to Haradinaj of Balaj's behaviour in Lluka and Prapaqan. On the 20th of July, 1998 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, Mr. Re, your computer presentation is steadily one or two items prior to what you are saying, that is rather confusing, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It is. Okay. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This is not an invitation to speak more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We're up to sighting number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have now on our screen, we have the swearing-in ceremony which is dated the 20th of July --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's sighting number 21. That's at the Baran swearing-in ceremony, and there is a video of that in evidence and the Trial Chamber has viewed it. Balaj is clearly present there with Haradinaj in attendance in the crowd. The next one is a meeting of Bislim Zyrapi from the KLA General Staff with Haradinaj in July 1998 in Irzniq. Sighting 23 is abducting Witness 1 and raping Witness 2, as pleaded in the last counts in the indictment, that occurred in early August 1998. 24, delivering or detaining the ECMM team and then delivering them to Haradinaj in Gllogjan, that was the 11th of August, 1998. Sighting 25, meeting with Haradinaj, Tahir Zemaj, and Witness 17 between the 11th and 20th of August, 1998. 26th, of course, was the evidence you heard of his moving Sanije Balaj's body from Lugu i Isufit to the canal in his black jeep, which was mid-August 1998, around the 15th or so. 27, mid-to-late August 1998, abducting Witness 4's Sister M in Ratishe. 28, meeting of village commanders with Haradinaj in Prapaqan, that's the 20th of August, 1998. 29, questioning Tush and Illira Frrokaj who were taken to a check-point in Gllogjan in August 1998. Sighting 30, training soldiers at the Gllogjan KLA headquarters in August 1998. 31, seen by a witness before leaving the village, Irzniq, that's late August 1998. And if you look at the last slide in that presentation it shows all of the sightings of Idriz Balaj which are in evidence over that period. The evidence against Balaj is overwhelming. He played an important and brutal role in persecuting the victims of the common criminal purpose. Turning now to the criminality accompanying some of the sightings of Toger, a.k.a., Balaj. In Counts 13 and 14 of the indictment, persecution, murder, abduction, imprisonment, and harassment of members of Witness 4's family in Ratis, I'm going to take you to this particular count to show Haradinaj's role in this and how it relates to the joint criminal enterprise and the common criminal purpose. Over a period of possibly five months between March and April 1998, Balaj, himself, his Black Eagles unit, and other KLA members harassed and terrorised Witness 4's family in Ratis before abducting and murdering his two sisters and their mother. The late father had been a state-employed forest ranger. A retired Serbian policeman was very close to the family. Consistent with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, before we continue, just to better be able to follow your submissions, you said five months between March and April --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Consistent with the pattern of persecutory attacks against those allegedly not supporting the KLA and supposedly collaborating with the Serbs, Balaj and KLA participants in the joint criminal enterprise viciously persecuted this family. They first came in late March 1998 around the 30th of March. They arrived late at night, some wore black clothes, some were uniformed, some wore masks. They said they belonged to a special unit and were searching the home for weapons because Witness 4's family had been licensed to possess fire-arms. Their presence absolutely terrified the family. Late at night several weeks later in mid-April 1998, Balaj returned bringing armed KLA soldiers under his command to the family home. He -- Witness 4 heard a soldier repeat the name Toger over and over. Balaj introduced himself to Witness 4's mother as Toger. He told the family -- he told her that each family member had to have a soldier in the army. He then abducted the oldest daughter, Sister S. About four days later, Toger briefly brought Sister S back before taking her away again. Toger and Sister S were both wearing black KLA special unit uniforms with KLA insignia. Sister S said she was staying at the old school in Rznic being used as a KLA base. The fourth visit to the house was in early May. One to two weeks later Toger dropped off Sister S, again she was wearing a black uniform, and she'd said as I'd described earlier, there was a prison in Rznic and Toger had ordered her to kill someone and threatened to kill her if she refused. She was afraid to give more details for fear that Toger, that is, Balaj, would harm her. Under Toger's orders she walked back towards Rznic, but later that day Toger came back and asked why she was late in returning. Witness 4 told Toger she had already left. The family never saw her again. The fifth visit was in late May 1998, about two to three weeks later. Witness 4 went to Ratis headquarters to ask for a permit to allow the family to travel. He was denied the permit, but shortly afterwards Balaj and other KLA soldiers came back to the family home, telling the mother she was not allowed to travel anywhere because her husband had worked for the Serbian authorities. He threatened to kill her if she tried to go anywhere. Now, that provides direct evidence of Balaj's persecutory intention. If that wasn't enough, there was a sixth visit in June 1998, in approximately June, when Balaj brought a group of armed soldiers to the home late one night. He questioned the mother about the whereabouts of the oldest son and he abducted her. He took her away and her family never saw her again. Her body was found at the canal in September. Balaj made a seventh visit. Late one night in mid-to-late August sometime after the mother's abduction, Balaj returned with several armed KLA soldiers and they broke down the family's door. Balaj dragged Sister M, that's Witness 4's sister. She was not even allowed to put on her shoes, dragged her through her room and out through the broken front door. Four or five days later the body was found by the side of the road about 5 or 6 kilometres away. Her throat was slit. She had been shot behind the ear and stabbed multiple times in the arms, back, and shoulder. Her right arm was extended above her head and her left hand grabbed the ground as if she was trying to get up before she died. Her leather jacket was found near her body, was bullet-ridden, and had 50 to 60 knife cuts. Her body -- her family buried the body near the house and then fled in fear to a relative's village. The Office of the Prosecutor later exhumed her body. An autopsy showed that multiple gun-shot wounds caused her death. Balaj or others acting with him murdered this woman; there is no other explanation, no other conclusion is available from the evidence. And from what you heard at trial, the only conclusion is that he murdered her with persecutory intention. But what is conclusive about his involvement is how and where the bodies were found. The bodies of the mother, R-11, and the sister, R-12, as you can see in the photo on the screen were found at the canal wall underneath the body of Sanije Balaj, that's body R-1. Their heads were next to each other and between them was a barbed-wire noose in between which long black hair and decaying human tissue was lodged. The canal wall above the bodies was perforated with bullet strikes. The bodies of the mother and the sister had severe injuries. The Sister S's body had multiple fractures consistent with gun-shot wounds. The mother's body had multiple fractures consistent with gun-shot wounds. There were bullets inside her body-bag and a bullet in her vertebrae. The similarity, and I return to the similarities, the similarity of these wounds on these bodies, their proximity, the cause of death, the bullets in the mother's body and the body-bag, and the bullet strikes on the wall are all consistent with execution on the spot. The blunt-trauma injuries and the barbed-wire noose containing the long black hair provide compelling evidence that one or both was tortured before execution. It's also significant that both died before Sanije Balaj's body was dumped on top of their remains by Balaj or someone acting for him in mid-August. This is entirely consistent with the dates and chronologies given by the witness. Your Honours, Toger is Balaj. The recognition evidence is incontestable and proves Balaj's identity as Toger beyond reasonable doubt. Witness 4 recognised Toger as Balaj from the seven "visits" that Balaj made to his family home. Toger, that is, Balaj, did nothing to hide his identity when committing these crimes. Another factor which indicates his authority and impunity, he wore the same clothes always, the black KLA special uniform worn by the Black Eagles, and he always seemed to command the other soldiers. Balaj and the other KLA members persecuted these family members because of their association and perceived collaboration with Serbian authorities. The three victims were all civilians. The victims were all murdered by gun-shot after Balaj abducted them. Their bodies and their story is intricately linked to what happened to Sanije Balaj. This young woman aged about 22 at the time of her death, her brutal and unnecessary death, proves a direct connection between Balaj and Haradinaj and other participants in the joint criminal enterprise to persecute. The evidence is that - and you heard this evidence - on the 12th of August, 1998, KLA military police officer Mete Krasniqi and others detained her at the Baran village check-point because her name was on a list of Albanians who should be stopped. And the slide shows where Baran is in connection to the other places in the indictment. She was interrogated in the Baran KLA military police headquarters in the school building. One of the interrogators, Idriz Gashi, Galani, who has been found guilty by a Kosovo court of her murder, took Sanije Balaj out announcing that he had found the names of Serbian police in her notebook and she had to be taken to Gllogjan for further questioning. Galani and military police member Avni Krasniqi then drove her towards Haradinaj's Gllogjan headquarters for further questioning. Both Mete and Avni Krasniqi were members of the Baran military police under Hasan Gashi's command. The Trial Chamber has heard evidence that Haradinaj appointed Galani, the murderer, the commander of Lugu i Drinit area. Avni Krasniqi testified that this appointment meant that Galani "had to be obeyed." Galani was also close to -- very close to Mete Krasniqi. On the way to Gllogjan, Galani Gashi took Sanije Balaj out of the car and murdered her by shooting her with his pistol. The Trial Chamber heard evidence from Avni Krasniqi who was present when Galani murdered this young woman. After the murder, which was very, very hard to conceal and later that day, Galani took Iber and Avni Krasniqi back and ordered them to bury the body. Exhibit P925 on the screen shows the site of the murder and burial. This murder incident soon became very widely known in that area and a few days later Haradinaj himself went to the home of Sanije Balaj's brother, Shaban, to offer his condolences. Mete Krasniqi told Haradinaj that Galani had killed, had murdered, Sanije Balaj. However, about three days later -- about three days after the murder Balaj, Toger, arrived in Baran in a black jeep with Galani, that's the murderer, and two other soldiers. The Trial Chamber heard evidence about -- very strong evidence about the identity and role of Balaj in disposing of the body. Galani ordered Balaj to take -- sorry, ordered Avni Krasniqi to help Balaj move the body to a safer place. Balaj took Avni and Iber Krasniqi and the soldiers to Lugu i Isufit, the place shown in that slide a moment ago. Balaj waited in his jeep while the others exhumed the body and put it in the back of his jeep. Balaj then took Iber and Avni Krasniqi back and he, Balaj, drove away with the body. The body was found at the canal near the bodies of Kemal Gashi and Zenun Gashi. Zenun Gashi being the Roma police officer on the KLA wanted list circulated on about the 12th of July, 1998. Balaj or someone acting at his direction must have taken the body there. There is no other explanation of how it came to be lying there on top of the other victims abducted by Balaj in the preceding months. As I mentioned earlier, her body as shown in the slide, Exhibit P418, was on top of the bodies of the mother and sister of Witness 4, that's R-11 and R-12, last seen in Balaj's custody before Balaj collected Sanije Balaj's body. As a suspected collaborator, Sanije Balaj was arrested and murdered pursuant to the common criminal enterprise. When you consider carefully all of the circumstances leading to the -- all the circumstances lead to the overwhelming conclusion that Haradinaj must be linked to the murder because of the circumstances described before and the system of persecution put in place. And the most obvious one here is his contribution by assisting in covering up this brutal murder. By the third day after her well-known murder, he must have known from Galani, Mete Krasniqi, or his trusted lieutenant in Baran, that's Din Krasniqi about where her body was. But while he was -- around the same time he was talking to his family -- sorry, talking to the family of the victim, Sanije Balaj, his right-hand man Balaj, Toger, was exhuming the body and taking it to the canal. The only reasonable inference is that Haradinaj ordered or at least, at the very least, approved of the removal of her body. That Balaj took the body to the canal was no secret at the time either. Haradinaj argues that he was not responsible for investigating the murder because it did not happen in his area and that he did not have prisons or courtrooms and the suspect seemed to have left the area. We ask you to reject this argument in its entirety; it is absolutely implausible. Haradinaj was the most powerful individual in the zone. Idriz Gashi, Galani, was his own appointee. Mete and Avni Krasniqi took their orders from Din Krasniqi and Haradinaj pursuant to de facto -- at least a de facto parallel command structure then in Baran. The only possible reason for taking Sanije Balaj's body to the canal, which he referred to as a "safer place" for her body was to conceal the truth about the detention and killing by KLA members. This act, too, is no coincidence. It was just another act in the pattern of persecution and murders committed against perceived collaborators. I turn now to the role of Lahi Brahimaj in the joint criminal enterprise. Brahimaj was second only to Haradinaj in power and prestige in the Dukagjini Zone KLA. He commanded the strategic KLA stronghold of Jablanica. As the evidence establishes, it was the first village in the Dukagjini area to establish a significant KLA force. Brahimaj also had a central role in establishing the KLA base in Gllogjan. He was a member of the KLA's General Staff. He was its finance director. He was its liaison between the General Staff and the Dukagjini Zone. He was Haradinaj's uncle and an important and respected KLA figure in the zone. Before the clash in Gllogjan between the KLA and Serbian forces on the 24th of March, Pjeter Shala, the feared Pjeter Shala and Idriz Balaj operated out of Jablanica, where Brahimaj was based. By the 30th of March, 1998, Jablanica was guarded and fortified with approximately 200 armed and trained KLA members under Brahimaj's command. Brahimaj, the evidence establishes, was a close associate of Haradinaj and contributed to organising and strengthening the KLA in the Dukagjini region. Such was their closeness that after Haradinaj's KLA forces withdrew from Gllogjan on the 24th of March, they went to Jablanica. Haradinaj who was wounded in the attack himself took refuge in Brahimaj's house. And Jablanica, just like Gllogjan, was strategically located along a main KLA corridor for the importation of arms, equipment, and soldiers from Albania. Haradinaj and Brahimaj coordinated this arming effort in which large groups of KLA soldiers travelled between Albania and Jablanica, and Brahimaj himself led groups across the border collecting weapons. On the 23rd of June, Brahimaj -- Haradinaj -- sorry, Brahimaj became Haradinaj's deputy commander but was dismissed a few weeks later apparently for unauthorised absences from the zone. Brahimaj used his personal authority to publicly promote the persecution of suspected collaborators and KLA opponents. An example was the persecution of villagers from Grabanice who supported the opposition LDK. These men became "wanted" by the KLA as the result of Brahimaj's public accusations against them. In late May 1998, Brahimaj and another KLA commander Alush Agushi intercepted and confronted a group of Grabanice villagers in Gllogjan and Peje who were fleeing their village to escape the Serbian forces. Brahimaj ordered the Gllogjan villagers not to assist the group and the Jablanica staff began looking for the men from Grabanice. They instructed them to turn the men into the KLA staff. Pjeter Shala and two other KLA members abducted two of them, Fadil Fazliu and Naser Lika in Zabelj, beat them, accused them of being traitors, and took them by force to Jablanica. Brahimaj was in charge of the KLA barracks detention centre -- I'm sorry, detention centre, in Jablanica. The barracks were established by at least March 1998. Exhibit P357, which will be on the screen, shows the detention centre located in the KLA barracks, which is on the right of this picture or to the left as you enter it. The purpose of this detention centre was to further the common criminal purpose by detaining, torturing, and killing alleged collaborators and KLA opponents. No evidence exists that the prison was used for any other purpose. In establishing and operating a notorious prison and personally committing acts of violence against perceived KLA opponents, Brahimaj supported and encouraged KLA members to make further attacks in furtherance of the common criminal purpose. Every prisoner known to be detained there during the indictment period was an alleged collaborator or was otherwise considered by virtue of ethnicity to be a KLA enemy or opponent. Brahimaj, as the Jablanica KLA commander, had overall command of the barracks and detention centre and took control of the detention, release, and treatment of Jablanica prisoners; and he had a virtually continuous presence at the detention centre. Such was his presence there that he even had his own room in the detention centre adjacent to a prison cell. The guards called him the commander. His permission was required for prisoners to be released. You've heard evidence of how he controlled access to the barracks by civilians. He had unfettered control over the fate of his prisoners. He had the power to select individuals for imprisonment and for beating. He had the power to have prisoners taken out of their cells for beating or interrogation and the power to order other KLA soldiers to beat prisoners. The KLA at Jablanica treated Serbian and Montenegrin prisoners, the absolute and automatic enemies of the KLA, with particular brutality. Witness 6 and a Kosovo Albanian civilian and Nenad Remistar, a Serb civilian, were abducted by the KLA at the same time and initially imprisoned and beaten together in the barracks office. Witness 6 was eventually released after many weeks of mistreatment, but Remistar was taken away and murdered after just 24 hours of detention. For three days, three Montenegrins and a Bosnian, also imprisoned, were beaten with baseball bats and stabbed with knives until they too were "soaked with blood" and spitting blood, at which they too were taken away, never to be seen again. Brahimaj directly encouraged mistreatment, acts of mistreatment, by his subordinates and made personal allegations of collaboration against prisoners. When he made one such allegation against Witness 3, Brahimaj handed Witness 3 a revolver and told him to kill himself because Brahimaj did not want to stain his hands with the prisoner's blood. Brahimaj actively sought out and punished Witness 3 after he initially escaped from detention. The prison was notorious. Witness 6's relatives found out that Witness 6 had been detained in Jablanica through word of mouth from local villagers. A relative went there every day and the guards would tell him how Witness 6 was doing. The Serbian DB and the VJ, that's the military, also knew about the KLA prison in Jablanica. They had information that kidnapped Serbs, Romas, and loyal Albanians were detained there. And I won't display it but Exhibit P981 provides details of what the DB knew at the time. Brahimaj carried out these activities openly in the midst of KLA barracks full of soldiers and the presence of other KLA members. His conduct demonstrated his total approval and encouragement of the general atmosphere of violence and terror towards alleged collaborators at the detention centre. Nenad Remistar, a Serb civilian, worked as a traffic policeman in Gjakove. He was a civilian for the purposes of an armed conflict. He took no active part in hostilities and was not a member of the Serbian forces. On the last day that his family saw him, on the 13th of June, 1998, he left home for work in a blue Opel Kadett vehicle wearing civilian clothes. His relatives became concerned after not hearing from him for several days and learned that he had not arrived at work. In late June some Kosovo Albanians told his father that Nenad Remistar had been imprisoned with a Catholic Albanian in Jablanica. Now, this is exactly what had happened. Witness 6 testified at page 5210: "Thank you. You mentioned the man whom you saw photographs in the Opel Kadett, the man you knew as Nenad, did you ever see him? "A. We were in the same room together that night. Both of us were beaten. We were tied up with a rope. We were, both of us tied up for 24 hours, until the next day in the morning. "Q. Did you actually see, yourself, with your own eyes Nenad being beaten? "A. Yes, both of us. "Q. And do you know who participated in the beating of Nenad? "A. Nazmi," that's Brahimaj, "with a group of soldiers that came. The soldiers were not always the same ones. They took turns. He stayed there for 24 hours." And then it goes on. "Q. What kind of condition was he in when the two soldiers came and took him? "A. He wasn't able to walk. Both of us actually had the same injuries. We were both beaten up. These two soldiers took him and I don't know what they did with him afterwards. "Q. Did you ever see Nenad again? "A. No." In relation to the three Bosnians and the Montenegrin, Witness 6 also testified at page 5277 about seeing them for about three days and their being beaten with baseball bats and being stabbed with knives and their clothes were full of blood, that's at 5277. Another prisoner detained at Jablanica was Pal Krasniqi, whose body was found at the canal. Pal Krasniqi sought to join the KLA in Jablanica, but the KLA instead accused him of spying for the Serbs, detained, tortured, and murdered him. Witness 6 testified of seeing him, of the last time he saw him at Jablanica. You can see a photograph of Pal Krasniqi at P334.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At page 5240 to 41 of the transcript, Witness 6 testified when asked to describe the condition Pal Krasniqi was in at Jablanica when last seen there. The question was: "What sort of condition was he in? What were his physical capabilities with as much detail as you can muster, please?" The answer was: "As a person is before he dies. "Q. Was there any blood on him? "A. Yes, there was blood on him. He was spitting blood. His body was all black and blue because of the beating, because of the -- sorry, swollen. He was lying down on the floor. I would bring him some water. He was in this shape for a week. Then I was released and left that place and I don't know what happened to him. "Q. Did you ever see him again? "A. No." The reason why he never saw him again was because Pal Krasniqi was murdered. His body, R-9, was found by the canal in a group of bodies visible along a section of the canal perforated with bullet-holes. The autopsy revealed fractures to his arms and legs which were entirely consistent with the evidence of the brutal beatings. The cause of death was multiple gun-shot wounds to the head, trunk, and upper limbs. The cause of death, the bullet-holes in the canal and his body had a scarf around it indicate that he was probably taken from the Jablanica detention centre to the canal wall and probably executed on the spot. The only conclusion in these circumstances that he was last seen close to death in the KLA's detention centre in Jablanica and his body was found in the KLA's mass grave site in the heart of KLA-controlled territory is that he was murdered by KLA members acting pursuant to the joint criminal enterprise. Another person whose murder was charged in the same count is Skender Kuci. The evidence was given that this prisoner at Jablanica detention centre was "beaten to a pulp." He was not in a position to get up let alone walk around in the courtyard. He'd got to the point where he used to pee in his pants. Witness 6 gave testimony about Lahi Brahimaj and Nazmi Brahimaj being present when the beatings occurred and their participation in the beatings of prisoners at the Jablanica detention centre. If I could just pause for a moment and just go through these slides relatively quickly showing Skender Kuci's abduction to Jablanica. Pal Krasniqi leaving Peje to join the KLA at Jabllanice. Witness 3's arrest in Zhabel, being taken to Jabllanice. Three tortured and beaten at Jabllanice. The escape of Witness 3, the death of Skender Kuci from his injuries and his burial at Jabllanice. And you can see on Exhibit P267, he was buried in the woods close to the Jablanica detention centre indicated by the red arrow, and the circle, the black circle, being the Jablanica KLA headquarters. In September 1998 Pal Krasniqi's remains were recovered by the canal, and his remains are shown in photograph 667.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I'm looking at the clock. I'd like to have a break until 6.00, and then I think 20 minutes remain for you, and I'm going to be strict in time because otherwise --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Not a problem. I'm well within -- well on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then, Mr. Emmerson, then you are invited or any of your colleagues to start for the last 40 minutes today so that we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, 20 minutes remaining for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we just look at the last slide on the screen. Before the break I said that in September 1998, Pal Krasniqi's remains were recovered by the canal. This slide shows that they were found near R-8, Velizar Stosic, and R-8/1, Zdravko Radunovic, and close to R-7, Sali Berisha, and R-4, Zenun Gashi. Zenun Gashi being on the KLA wanted list, that's Exhibit P667. I turn now to another count in which Kosovar Albanian civilians on KLA wanted lists were abducted by KLA members and ended up by the canal, and that's the case of Nurije and Istref Krasniqi, paragraph 83 of the indictment in Counts 21 and 22. You can see their photos in P347 and 346. In 1998 Istref was 60, Nurije 56 or 58. On the 12th of July, 1998, four armed KLA soldiers took them from their home in Turjak. They were suspected Serbian collaborators. Rumours had circulated in Turjak that they were "sons of Bosnians and collaborators to the Serbs." On about the 10th of July, KLA commander Rrustem Tetaj had -- and armed KLA soldiers had arrived at their home in two black jeeps. Tetaj had introduced himself as Ramush Haradinaj's deputy. Two days later at a meeting of the Baran valley command in the house of the commander, Din Krasniqi appointed by Haradinaj, a list was circulated of people who were wanted by Din Krasniqi and the KLA. The list is on the screen at the moment and it shows two women collaborators from Turjak. Now, the evidence shows that one of these had to be Nurije because of the circumstances of how her name came to be put there. It referred to her son who had been shot in the neck and Din Krasniqi had actually treated -- he was a doctor, had treated him for his wounds. Now, Witness 17 said the existence of the collaborators was well-known to the people at the meeting. And the same afternoon of the meeting and the circulation of the list, the two Krasniqis returned home. KLA commander Tetaj and KLA soldiers came and took another person Smajl Gashi from Turjak to Haradinaj's Gllogjan KLA headquarters for interrogation, but at about midnight Tetaj sent Gashi back with KLA soldiers to show them where the Krasniqis' house was. These KLA soldiers then put Istref and Nurije Krasniqi into a black jeep, saying that they were taking them to Gllogjan on Tetaj's orders. Rumours of their abduction and murder circulated, and Tetaj -- sorry, and Tahir Zemaj, the FARK commander, appointed Fadil Nimonaj to investigate their disappearance. Selca concluded that Tetaj, the KLA had abducted this couple and Tetaj was pivotal to what happened. On the 15th of July, Din Krasniqi told a relative that he, Krasniqi, had been to KLA headquarters in Gllogjan and was told that they were interrogated there and released. Now, Selca's contemporaneous official notes corroborate this, it was on the screen a moment ago, saying that Imer Krasniqi had been taken from the village of Turjak for an interview regarding his collaboration with the Serbian police in several other cases. What happened to this couple? After they were abducted by KLA soldiers the names -- the name of one appearing on a KLA wanted list, the other it was found was taken there for suspected collaboration, their bodies, R-14 and R-15, were found on the 12th of September near the canal wall. Their bodies were under a gravel pit close to other corpses. Both had multiple gun-shot wounds. Gun-shot wounds caused the death of both. Their bodies were underneath the spot where there were bullet marks or bullet strikes in the wall, which is consistent with death by execution at that particular spot. The couple were accused of collaboration and named on a KLA wanted list, either created or approved by the Baran valley KLA command. KLA soldiers took them to Haradinaj's Gllogjan headquarters on his deputy's orders. Their executed bodies were found next to other KLA victims. Your Honours, the only inference available from this evidence singly and in its totality is that they were murdered by KLA members acting pursuant to the joint criminal enterprise. And you can see from this slide that their remains were also found in the vicinity of the body of R-10, Vukosava Markovic, the elderly Serb sister who disappeared in April 1998 in KLA-controlled territory in the Ratishe-Gllogjan area. Another example ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- is out of the death of Zenun Gashi and Misin Berisha which is pleaded in Counts 19 and 20 of the indictment. Zenun Gashi was a retired police officer. His family feared that because of his collaboration with the KLA he would become a target of the KLA -- because of his, sorry, feared collaboration with the Serbs by virtue of having been a police officer, he would become a target. Now, the events prove their fears were entirely justified. On around the 1st of August, 1998, KLA military police members abducted Zenun Gashi from his home and took him to Mete Krasniqi at the KLA headquarters in Baran on the orders of Faton Mehmetaj. Faton Mehmetaj, you will recall, had been appointed to that position by Haradinaj. As you can see on the slide P8, the slide showing in front of you, Zenun Gashi's name is on the list of collaborators circulated at the meeting on 12th of July, together with his son. You can also see number 9, Misin Berisha, a Roma person from Gllogjan. Two months later the bodies of Misin Berisha, his sons Xhevet and Sali, and Zenun Gashi were found together at the canal wall. Misin Berisha, a Roma civilian, a supporter of Ibrahim Rugova, the opposition, lived in Gllogjan, Peje, with his sons. The circumstantial evidence of what happened to Zenun Gashi, how he died supports the direct evidence of his abduction and mistreatment by the KLA. The KLA Baran commander Din Krasniqi told Witness 17 that Faton Mehmetaj ordered Zenun Gashi transported to Gllogjan. This is of course where Mehmetaj and Haradinaj shared an office. Din Krasniqi said that Zenun Gashi would be killed by the KLA secret police if taken there. Witness 17 attempted to obtain Gashi's release. He was told they'd been released. Din Krasniqi said that Gashi would be "liquidated" if re-arrested. This is exactly what happened, fitting the pattern of persecution of KLA enemies. When Witness 17 asked Din Krasniqi to have him released again, Din Krasniqi confirmed to Witness 17 with a lateral cutting motion across his throat that Zenun Gashi was dead, and the forensic evidence supports that. Another victim was Sejd Noci whose body was found at the canal. He was a Serb civilian Kosovar from Dujak last seen being delivered to a KLA check-point near Junik in July. His body was recovered in parts next to a steep slope about 650 metres downstream from the canal near that of Hajrullah Gashi, R-22 and Jusuf Hoxha, R-23, both of whom had disappeared in June or July 1998, Jusuf Hoxha being a police informer. The evidence has proved that this attack against civilians was widespread. Within the zone controlled by Haradinaj's KLA, all the victims came within a very geographically compact area. One slide which we have handed out in advance shows the systematic nature of the attack over six months, the locations of the bodies at the canal shows the systematic nature of their disposal. If you look at the slides on the screen, they're divided by colour. The first one is of ethnic Serb and Montenegrin victims, and you can see where they disappeared from throughout the indictment period. The next one is of Roma Egyptian, Ashkali victims in green. The third slide is of Roman Catholic victims. The fourth slide is of perceived collaborators and KLA opponents. The names of all the victims in the indictment are listed on these slides. When you put them all together and you look at where the dots are and where Gllogjan is, where Jablanica is, where the canal is, you can see how widespread or systematic the attack was over that particular period. Haradinaj, Balaj, and Brahimaj and others jointly participated in the campaign of terrorising and persecuting civilians. They succeeded in their aim of cleansing Serbs from the Dukagjini area and terrorising others into submission. If you look at the canal and the victims found there in the slide, it shows where they came from, running through them quickly. And if you look at the last slide of all victims found at the canal site, it shows exactly where they were found throughout the zone between March -- where they lived between March and April -- sorry, March and August 1998. The Trial Chamber has heard witnesses give direct evidence of each accused personally committing the crimes charged in the indictment, crimes such as rape, torture, and cruel treatment. The evidence of their personal involvement in some crimes when combined with the organized nature of the KLA's activities in the context of the sheer scale of the crimes committed within such a geographically small area proves their participation in the enterprise. The evidence against each is in our submission overwhelming. The accused participated in a joint criminal enterprise which claimed the lives of at least 40 victims. It ruined the lives of others, the families of the deceased, the victims of torture, rape, cruel treatment, and the other crimes. The Prosecution has charged only three of its participants. Others, including Haradinaj's brother Daut and Brahimaj's brother Nazmi are not charged. But it's worth the Trial Chamber going back to the brief and pausing to consider the evidence, what the evidence has proved about their action; that is, Nazmi Brahimaj's central role in the persecution at the Jablanica detention centre, beating Witness 6 with a baseball bat so viciously that the victim's face was swollen and he lost consciousness, the death of Skender Kuci, and the involvement of Daut Haradinaj in the participation, torture and detention of the Stojanovic brothers in April 1998. The actions of these and others are described in paragraph 285 to 335 of the brief. Each accused, Your Honours, had an integral role in the common criminal purposes of the joint criminal enterprise. Haradinaj as the overall commander of those who committed the crimes, Balaj as commander of the Black Eagles, Brahimaj in running the detention centre at Jablanica. The actions of the accused were brutal. They acted according to a common criminal purpose to persecute. Their victims were targeted and attacked because of their ethnicity, political persuasion, or religion. But the tragedy of these events, the wasted lives, ruined lives, those left without homes or loved ones is that the attacks were so unnecessary. The elderly Serbs who remained behind in Ratis and Dashinoc posed no threat to the political or military aims of the KLA. There was no need to murder them, but it was their presence there that offended those participating in the common criminal purpose. There was no need to detain and torture Haradinaj's family neighbours, Witness 4's family posed no threat, military or political to the KLA. As in any situation where the minority has political power, the political arm, the LPK, the KLA, would eventually have won the political struggle perhaps without other political parties. The persecution which the Prosecution has overwhelming proved beyond reasonable doubt was tragically unnecessary, and these crimes, the 40 murders and the numerous other crimes pleaded and proved, deserve serious condemnation and severe punishment. The Prosecution has proved the participation of each accused beyond reasonable doubt. In the circumstances, the Prosecution proving its case and the participation of the accused, the Trial Chamber should impose sentences of 25 years' imprisonment on each of Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj, and Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re. Mr. Emmerson, are you ready --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to present closing arguments. You'll be the first one --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's the plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of Defence counsel. You know that the Chamber leaves the distribution of time in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Towards the beginning of his address this afternoon, Mr. Re criticised the Haradinaj Defence and he criticised us for urging the Trial Chamber to subject the evidence on each count individually to close and searching scrutiny. He said the Trial Chamber must look at the totality rather than concerning itself with shortcomings in the evidence on the individual counts. In effect, he says that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. He's right in one matter. He's right to identify a difference of approach between the Prosecution and the Defence. We say that it is only once the Trial Chamber has determined the findings of fact that can properly be reached on the evidence adduced for each count on the indictment that it is possible to stand back and see what the overall picture reveals. Of course those counts must be viewed in their context, but the broad-brush approach which the Prosecution is driven to advocate is, in our submission, no substitute for a methodical evaluation of the evidence. And when the evidence is examined critically and methodically, it becomes clear that the entire edifice of inference which the Prosecution has tried to painstakingly to build ultimately rests on foundations of sand. At the end of his submissions Mr. Re made the surprising submission to the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution had proved the personal participation of each accused in counts on the indictment beyond reasonable doubt. The indictment contains five pairs of counts which allege that Mr. Haradinaj personally committed, instigated, or aided and abetted the commission of the crimes alleged. As Mr. Re knows well, as the trial unfolded each of those allegations fell away. The Prosecution has called no reliable evidence at all of the personal participation of Ramush Haradinaj in any of the counts alleged on the indictment. In its closing brief the Prosecution faintly suggests that the Trial Chamber could conclude that Mr. Haradinaj was present during the alleged ill-treatment of Witness 38, which is the subject of Counts 1 and 2, but the argument is not put forward with any real enthusiasm and it got no mention at all in Mr. Re's closing submission and the reason is obvious: The identification evidence could hardly have been any less reliable and there was serious grounds to question the credibility of Witness 38's testimony. Her identification was based upon an observation of a man she claims to have seen in profile across a distance of 30 metres at a time when she was traumatised and her view was obstructed by trees and bushes. She claims to have recognised Mr. Haradinaj several months later when she saw him on television, but she failed to mention this to anyone for seven and a half years despite the fact that she'd made a detailed statement to the MUP in 2002. Her identification was uncorroborated by Witness 58 and her testimony was inconsistent in important respects with her prior statements. There is no basis on which the Chamber could safely conclude that the man she claims to have seen was Ramush Haradinaj. For reasons which I'll come to in more detail in due course, we submit that the same is true of the allegation that Mr. Haradinaj was present and stood by at the time of the assault on the Stojanovic brothers and Veselin Stijovic. The recognition evidence on Counts 3 and 4 is manifestly unreliable by any objective standard, and I will, if I may, deal with that in more detail when I come to those particular counts. But as to the remaining counts, the Prosecution has effectively withdrawn each of the allegations made against Mr. Haradinaj personally, either because the evidence called was plainly unreliable, or because no evidence was called at all. And so the starting point for any analysis of the case against Ramush Haradinaj must be that there is no reliable evidence of his personal involvement in any of the crimes alleged. The case against Mr. Haradinaj rests, and rests solely, on the allegation that he was party to a joint criminal enterprise and it depends, and depends exclusively, on circumstantial evidence. In the course of my submissions, I am going to address that allegation under three broad headings. I am going to deal first with the allegation that he was party to a joint criminal enterprise to persecute Serb civilians. In short, we say the evidence does not prove the existence of any such agreement and that there is no reliable evidence that Mr. Haradinaj authorised, condoned, or acquiesced in any of the crimes alleged on the indictment. In the second part of my submissions, I'm going to deal with the allegation that Mr. Haradinaj participated in a policy of ill-treatment and summary execution directed at perceived collaborators and opponents. We say that his conduct and his interventions point to precisely the opposite conclusion. And finally, I'm going to address the Prosecution's arguments concerning the finding of bodies at the Lake Radoniq canal site and the inferences which can properly be drawn from that evidence. Mr. Re has put it at the centre of his submissions, and I am going to deal with it in some detail. But in a sentence or two, we say that the Prosecution has entirely failed to prove the allegation that this was a KLA execution site or that it was a dumping ground located in territory exclusively controlled by the KLA. We say there are serious questions to be asked about the integrity of the investigation, and we say that when the evidence in respect of each individual is examined the Prosecution case theory falls apart. But most important of all, there is no evidence whatsoever to connect Mr. Haradinaj to any of those deaths. Before I develop those submissions, I want to start by saying a few words about the concept of leadership in the context of the emergence of the KLA in Western Kosovo during 1998. I think it's probably fair to say that Mr. Re conceded that the real thrust of the Prosecution's case against Mr. Haradinaj comes down to a single proposition; that is, that because he was a prominent and charismatic commander, he must be taken to have authorised the crimes alleged on the indictment. We submit that this is the fallacy which lies at the heart of the Prosecution case. The evidence shows that the KLA emerged as a movement in the Dukagjin region, over a period of time, without any of the formal command structures of a conventional army. The backdrop to the events alleged on the indictment is, of course, the devastating series of attacks by Serb forces on Likoshan and Prekaze. The evidence shows clearly the enormous fear and insecurity felt in the Albanian civilian population. Following the assault on Gllogjan on the 24th of March and in the context of the build-up of Serb forces in the area which were poised to strike at any time with potentially devastating consequences for civilians, more and more villages began to start organizing their own flimsy defences. Some of them called themselves KLA; others called themselves territorial defences or village defences. But none of these people were soldiers. They were farmers or shopkeepers by day and fighters by night. They were all unpaid volunteers. There was no central command, no formal recruitment procedure or vetting process, and no effective means of enforcing military discipline. This was a movement of terrified Albanian civilians that grew out of existing village structures and loyalties. The Defence doesn't dispute that Mr. Haradinaj made efforts, with others, to try to coordinate these autonomous groupings into some sort of cohesive fighting force. It's plain that he emerged as a figurehead for the resistance movement following the failure of the Serb forces to eliminate the Haradinaj family on the 24th of March. But the reality of his leadership position bears no real comparison to the position of a conventional military commander, and that's why so many witnesses have spoken in terms of a horizontal rather than a vertical system of organization. When the first serious attempt was made to try to coordinate these autonomous village groupings into a joint command on the 26th of May, Ramush Haradinaj was in reality little more than a prominent village commander with a strong reputation as a fighter, a man others were prepared to rally behind. The leaders of this emerging movement borrowed the language of a conventional army as a means of encouraging cohesion and boosting morale. Titles were given to people and structures agreed on, which bore only the most passing resemblance to the realities on the ground. The indictment consists of a series of unconnected crimes alleged to have occurred in different places across the indictment region, at different times during the indictment period. In most cases, the perpetrators are unidentified. The crimes alleged do not, in our submission, establish any clear pattern or system capable of amounting to a joint criminal enterprise. And for the Prosecution to suggest that merely because he emerged over time as the leader of the KLA in the Dukagjin region, Mr. Haradinaj must have authorised or condoned the commission of these crimes is, in our submission, both illogical and inconsistent with the evidence. Equally unsubstantiated is the allegation that Mr. Haradinaj sought to exclude and then subordinate FARK for purposes somehow connected with the joint criminal enterprise alleged on the indictment. The evidence shows that following the unexpected arrival of FARK forces in the Dukagjin region, a series of meetings took place in which the two sides expressed serious and legitimate differences of opinion on the appropriate way of deploying the FARK officers. Neither side wanted to back down. But Witness 17, who took part in those meetings, said that Mr. Haradinaj was "controlled and orderly" throughout, and that his approach to the discussions as a whole was "constructive and moderate," those are his words. It says something about the way in which the Prosecution presents its case that Mr. Re chose not to draw your attention to the words of Witness 17, who took part in the meetings, but instead to rely on the complete distortion put forward by Witness 29, who did not take part in the meetings. Despite two instances of confrontation on the 4th and the 10th of July, the FARK forces were successfully integrated into the KLA through the formation of three mixed brigades on the 12th of July, less than three weeks after they first arrived in Kosovo. And Witness 17 confirmed in terms that following the establishment of the brigades, the relationship between Mr. Haradinaj and Mr. Zemaj became closer. The incident on the 4th of July in Gllogjan was an ugly and regrettable confrontation between soldiers, but it is not evidence of any policy to persecute civilians and it is not alleged as a count on the indictment. For reasons set out in our closing brief, we submit that the testimony of Witness 29 about this incident was unreliable in a number of respects, just as his testimony about the meetings that took place when FARK arrived was manifestly unreliable. But however this confrontation erupted, the evidence shows that it was swiftly resolved at a meeting between Tahir Zemaj and Ramush Haradinaj the following day. Taken in the context of the constructive negotiations that Witness 17 says took place before and taken in the context of the constructive negotiations and solution that was reached within days thereafter, this single incident can hardly provide evidence of an intention to exclude FARK forces for some unspecified purpose connected with the alleged JCE. But perhaps the clearest indication of Mr. Haradinaj's overall approach is the fact that he permitted the FARK to occupy the Prapaqan barracks which had been set up and financed by the KLA and were the best facility they had available. Those were not the actions of a commander who was seeking to exclude or subordinate FARK for some criminal purpose. On the 21st of August, following the routing of the KLA in Gllogjan, Mr. Haradinaj resigned as zone commander. Far from seeking to subordinate FARK, he agreed to serve under the command of Tahir Zemaj. The reversal of that decision a fortnight later was on the evidence not Mr. Haradinaj's doing; the evidence shows that it was the result of a power struggle between the General Staff and the government in exile, each of which wanted their own man in command of the strategically important Dukagjin region. The suggestion that the problems surrounding the integration of FARK are somehow evidence of Mr. Haradinaj's participation in the joint criminal enterprise alleged on the indictment is completely and utterly contrived. We submit that there's nothing in it at all and that the Trial Chamber should reject it out of hand. I want to come now to the allegation that Mr. Haradinaj was the architect of a campaign to persecute and forcibly expel Serb civilians. The evidence shows that a relatively small number of isolated crimes were committed against Serb civilians during the indictment period. In most cases, there is no evidence of the identity of the perpetrators, and the Prosecution has adduced no reliable or credible evidence whatsoever to show that Mr. Haradinaj ever authorised or condoned the commission of any of these crimes. It's undoubtedly true that weapons were much more freely available to Albanians at this time. That was an inevitable part of the defensive preparations that all sections of the Albanian civilian community were making for the anticipated attacks by Serb forces. But by no means all of these weapons were in the hands of people who considered themselves to be members of the KLA. There is clear and unequivocal evidence that unaffiliated groups and individuals also took part in trips across the border to bring weapons back to their village defences. The increasing availability of weapons provides a number of possible explanations for isolated attacks on Serb civilians. During April, many Serb families moved from their homes in rural areas of Western Kosovo for their own safety. By and large they moved to the major towns which remained solidly under Serb control. But the evidence doesn't establish that this exodus was the result of any organized campaign of expulsion. There is no evidence that people were systematically ordered from their homes. They left because they were living in isolated areas with a predominantly ethnic Albanian population. Many witnesses ascribed their sense of fear to the increasing visibility of armed Albanian villagers, particularly at night, driving around, setting up vehicle check-points, shooting in the air. It may very well be that people fled in fear of this, but that does not establish that there was anything amounting to a campaign of persecution. A number of specific incidents appear to have contributed to the sense of insecurity among the Serb civilian population at this time, such as the shooting of Slobodan Praskevic on the 2nd of March and the attacks on the homes of a small number of individuals of Serb ethnicity. But the evidence falls far short of proving that those isolated incidents were part of any coordinated attack by the KLA. According to Zoran Stijovic, for example, the shooting of Slobodan Praskevic was nothing to do with the KLA. Despite popular misconceptions that this was a KLA assassination, the police investigation established conclusively that the killing was committed for purely private reasons. It's a good illustration of the potential for incidents of that nature to be misconstrued. Similarly, Marijana Andjelkovic testified that the attack in Cermjan on the house of Radenko Fatic was carried out by one of his neighbours; and Miloica Vlahovic testified that his father had seen a group of neighbours on a tractor firing guns in the air outside his house. None of this establishes a policy of persecution, but in the fevered atmosphere that followed the attack on the 24th of March, these incidents were taken as a sign that open conflict was about to erupt. And it's against that background of confusion and disorganization that the counts alleged on the indictment fall to be judged. There are ten allegations of the ill-treatment or murder of individuals of Serb ethnicities, and I am going to say a word or two about each of them but perhaps a little more about the first. Counts 3 and 4 concern the assault on the Stojanovic brothers and Veselin Stijovic. This attack wasn't evidence of any campaign of ethnic persecution. These individuals were targeted not because they were Montenegrin but because of their family's perceived involvement in the devastating offensive against Gllogjan. It was inevitable that the people in the village would feel a deep sense of anger against those they thought were responsible for an attack that had claimed three young lives, destroyed many homes, and led to mass arrests and ill-treatment. The evidence shows clearly that there was a widespread perception in the village that the Stojanovic family had provided the information which led the Serb forces to attack Gllogjan. Predrag Stojanovic was a police officer and he took part in the offensive; indeed, he was involved in the incident at the village school. The Stojanovic family home was used as a military facility on the day, and Mijat Stojanovic testified that he was expecting retaliation from the villagers. Indeed, that's why the Serb police warned the family to leave the area after the 24th of March. The attack on those men was a spontaneous convulsion of violence by the villagers of Gllogjan, whose homes and families had come under attack. Plainly, it wasn't pre-planned. It plainly occurred opportunistically when word spread that the Stojanovic brothers had returned. Veselin Stijovic and Mijat Stojanovic both testified that the whole village seemed to be turning on them, that people came out of the fields and out of their homes to join in the attack. Many of those involved, they said, were youngsters who would have been contemporaries of the three teenagers killed on the 24th of March. None of this is to excuse what happened, but it does place the incident in its proper context. This wasn't the first Salvo in some planned campaign of violence against the Serb civilian population on the grounds of their ethnicity; it was a spontaneous reaction to the perceived involvement of these particular individuals in the devastating attack on Gllogjan. As to the allegation that Ramush Haradinaj stood by and let it happen, we submit that the identification evidence is manifestly unreliable. Each of the alleged sightings depends upon peripheral vision in the most traumatic of circumstances. Mijat Stojanovic claims to have caught sight of Mr. Haradinaj standing on the road to his house as the three men were being marched into the village. They had been ordered to keep their hands in the air, to keep their heads down, and not to look to the left or right. The alleged recognition is based on a fleeting glimpse in stressful and difficult circumstances over a distance of more than 70 metres. He later claimed to have caught sight of Mr. Haradinaj again as he was leaving the KLA headquarters, but this sighting too was brief and occurred in equally traumatic circumstances. The alleged recognition by Dragoslav Stojanovic was, if anything, even less reliable. Leaving aside for a moment the fact that his account -- that he responded by saying that he did not recognise the man in question, leaving that entirely to one side for a moment, looking solely at the objective circumstances, Dragoslav Stojanovic claims to have recognised Mr. Haradinaj while he was lying prone on the floor, face-down, slipping in and out of consciousness. Tellingly, he said that he couldn't provide any description of the other men who were there at the time because he was face-down and, in his words, hardly able to have a proper look. All of this Tribunal's jurisprudence warns, and warns clearly, of the danger of relying on identification evidence of this poor quality. The fact that these alleged identifications involve a claim of recognition does not render them, in our submission, any less vulnerable to error. Although the Stojanovic family lived next door to the Haradinajs, neither witness had seen Ramush Haradinaj for years. Even in recognition cases the opportunity for reliable observation is critical. An unobstructed and clear view of the subject, over a reasonable period of time, and a real and recent familiarity with the person's features are prerequisites before any recognition evidence could be accepted as reliable. As the leading English case of Turnbull points out, mistakes are made even in the recognition of close friends and relatives. It is notoriously difficult to evaluate the reliability of identification or recognition evidence by the demeanour of the witness. That's why the international jurisprudence consistently speaks of the need for objective criteria, and applying any set of objective criteria, it is clear that these identifications fall far short of the quality required for a conviction on the criminal standard of proof. But the difficulties with this identification evidence don't end there. In Kupreskic, the Appeals Chamber specifically drew attention to the additional risk which arises where a delayed assertion of memory is coupled with a clear possibility that the witness has been influenced by suggestions from others. Those words apply with their full force to the evidence of Mijat and Dragoslav Stojanovic. In conversations with Veselin Stijovic, both men named the people they recognised as having been involved on the 18th of April; neither of them mentioned Ramush Haradinaj. A week after the incident, Mijat Stojanovic was interviewed by Marijana Andjelkovic and by a Serbian magazine called "Ilustrovana Politika." In both interviews he gave a list of people that he recognised, but in neither case did he mention the name of Ramush Haradinaj. This delayed assertion of memory carries a particular risk in the present case because the Stojanovic family had close connections with the Serb security forces and because they hold Mr. Haradinaj responsible for the loss of their home. In short, we submit that there is no reliable evidence that Mr. Haradinaj was present on the 18th of April, that the application of any set of objective standards requires a conclusion that this evidence falls short, and that there is no basis to conclude that he permitted the ill-treatment alleged in Counts 3 and 4 to occur. I see the time. I am going to move on to another topic and I wonder if that might be a convenient moment.
